papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) promise improved cardiovascular risk stratification, but most validation derives from UK or Nordic biobanks. The transferability of these scores to Central European populations and their incremental value over classical risk factors in routine care remain unestablished. OBJECTIVES: To determine whether a coronary PRS derived from external European data transfers to a Polish primary-care population and adds discrimination for prevalent cardiovascular disease beyond classical risk factors. METHODS: In the nationwide Polish LIPIDOGEN2015 primary-care cohort, we derived PRS for coronary heart disease, myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke from FinnGen data with continuous shrinkage priors and applied them to imputed genotypes. We compared allele frequencies of 1397 unrelated participants with a non-Finnish European (NFE) reference and, in 1328 participants with clinical data, related the PRS to coronary artery disease (CAD), MI and stroke recorded at baseline and to a composite including death during follow-up, with and without classical risk factors or SCORE2. RESULTS: Allele frequencies correlated with the NFE reference (r = 0.97). Per standard deviation (SD), the coronary PRS was associated with prevalent CAD (odds ratio 1.36, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.67) and the composite endpoint (1.26, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.51), as were two validated genome-wide scores. Adding it to classical risk factors changed the area under the curve (AUC) for the composite endpoint by 0.0017 (95% CI -0.0005 to 0.0076), from 0.860 to 0.861; results with SCORE2 were similar. The study had 80% power for odds ratios per SD of 1.31 (CAD) and 1.27 (composite). CONCLUSIONS: A coronary PRS derived from external European data retains its association with prevalent CAD without re-derivation in this Polish primary-care cohort but, in this cross-sectional, event-limited sample, adds little discrimination to classical risk factors. Its value for predicting future events in this setting remains to be tested against incident outcomes.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVES: To investigate associations between early life infections, antibiotic exposure and juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), and to explore associations between genetic susceptibility to JIA and infection frequency, and potential gene–environment interactions. METHODS: We used data from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study (MoBa) and the Danish National Birth Cohort (DNBC). JIA was identified through national patient registries and chart reviews. Main exposures were prospectively parent-reported infection frequencies during 0–18 months, categorised into quartiles. Adjusted ORs (aORs) with 95% CIs were estimated by logistic regression and pooled using random-effects meta-analyses. papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Large-scale genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of genetic loci associated with kidney function. However, most polygenic risk score models for kidney function were developed in European populations, limiting their accuracy in non-European groups. This study aimed to validate the clinical utility of polygenic risk scores for kidney function decline in the Japanese general population. METHODS: We analyzed the Shika resident cohort cross-sectional and the Toshiba worker cohort prospectively to construct polygenic risk score models based on GWAS data from Japanese populations incorporating 344,577 and 352,151 genetic variants, respectively. The primary outcome was kidney function decline, defined as eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2. With adjustments for traditional risk factors, multivariate logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to assess associations between the polygenic risk score and kidney function decline. RESULTS: In the Shika resident cohort (n = 895, mean age 62 years), 157 participants (18%) had eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2; each standard deviation (SD) increase in the polygenic risk score conferred 55% higher odds (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.28-1.89). In the Toshiba worker cohort (n = 6,769, mean age 40 years), 1,593 participants (24%) developed eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 over median 8.3-year follow-up; each SD increase in the polygenic risk score was associated with 16% higher risk (HR 1.16, 95% CI 1.10-1.22). Adding the polygenic risk score to clinical models was associated with improved integrated discrimination in both cohorts, but the overall improvement in predictive ability was limited. CONCLUSIONS: The polygenic risk score was independently associated with kidney function decline beyond established risk factors and was associated with modestly improved risk prediction accuracy in Japanese populations, supporting its potential utility for personalized chronic kidney disease management.

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Sleep and dementia are complex phenotypes shaped by genetic and environmental factors, but the genetic contribution of sleep to dementia risk remains unclear. This study examined associations of both phenotypic and genetically predicted sleep traits and their interaction with dementia risk. METHODS: Data were drawn from the Screening Across the Lifespan Twin study (1998 to 2002) within the Swedish Twin Registry. Phenotypic sleep traits included sleep duration, insomnia, snoring, daytime sleepiness, chronotype, daytime napping, and a composite sleep score. Corresponding polygenic scores (PGSs) were derived from publicly available genome-wide association study summary statistics. Dementia diagnosis was obtained from national registers. Cox proportional hazards models estimated risk, excluding cases diagnosed within 10 years of baseline to reduce reverse causation. RESULTS: Among 13,087 individuals (mean age 70.27; 1541 dementia diagnosis cases), longer sleep duration (hazard ratio [HR] 0.93; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.86 to 1.00; p = 0.04) was associated with lower dementia risk over 13.42 years in models adjusted for sociodemographic and lifestyle behavioral factors. In within-pair analyses, this association was attenuated. Among 16,164 genotyped individuals (mean age 55.32; 559 cases), a one-standard deviation higher PGS for daytime napping (HR 1.12; 95% CI: 1.01 to 1.23; p = 0.03) was associated with higher dementia risk over 16.01 years. In 3133 individuals with both data types (mean age 66.79 years; 377 cases), this association persisted independently of phenotypic napping (HR 1.17; 95% CI: 1.03 to 1.33; p = 0.02), with no interaction observed. DISCUSSION: Genetic liability to daytime napping in midlife may reflect a distinct vulnerability for dementia, whereas napping in late-life may serve a compensatory or restorative function.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is a clinically used biomarker of hepatobiliary injury and alcohol exposure, yet accumulating evidence links higher GGT to systemic cardiometabolic and other comorbidities. Although large-scale GWAS have defined many GGT-associated loci in European-ancestry cohorts, the genetic architecture of GGT, its cross-trait liability, and the translational utility of GGT polygenic risk remain insufficiently characterized in East Asian populations. METHODS: We performed a cross-biobank genetic analysis of GGT in East Asian populations. We conducted a GWAS of circulating GGT in 46,704 Han Taiwanese participants from the CMUH Biobank and integrated GWAS summary statistics from East Asian biobanks to quantify cross-trait genetic correlations with cardiometabolic phenotypes. Putative causal effects were evaluated using univariable and BMI-adjusted multivariable Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses. Translational utility was assessed by constructing a GGT polygenic risk score (PRS) and testing its associations across the clinical phenome and in BMI-stratified time-to-event analyses of incident type 2 diabetes (T2D). RESULTS: In a Han Taiwanese GWAS (n = 46,704), we identified 18 genome-wide significant loci for circulating GGT, including five putative previously unreported Han Taiwanese signals at RBMS3, APBB2, AC091905.2, CCDC88C, and PML after comparison with prior GGT GWAS and the GWAS Catalog. Across East Asian biobanks, GGT shared genetic liability with ALT/AST and cardiometabolic traits, including T2D, adiposity, blood pressure, and lipids. MR supported causal effects of higher GGT liability on ALT/AST, and T2D-related signals persisted after BMI-adjusted multivariable MR. A GGT PRS showed pleiotropic PheWAS associations and stratified incident T2D within BMI strata consistently. CONCLUSION: This cross-biobank study refined and extended the East Asian genetic architecture of circulating GGT and demonstrated broad shared liability with cardiometabolic traits, alongside BMI-independent causal signals for hepatic injury biomarkers and persisting T2D-related effects. These findings support the use of GGT genetics and polygenic risk for comorbidity stratification and genomics-informed risk prediction in precision medicine.

papers.title: How inherited variation shapes human disease trajectories
papers.abstract: Although inherited variation is fixed at birth, its effects on health change with age and differ between common and rare variants. Here, we introduce Mendelnoulli, a longitudinal model that combines the age-dependent effects of polygenic and monogenic variation on health records, separating how much disease each individual accumulates overall from diseases to which they are prone. Mendelnoulli further allows polygenic and monogenic components to exert different influences on latent disease traje…
papers.abstract_full: Although inherited variation is fixed at birth, its effects on health change with age and differ between common and rare variants. Here, we introduce Mendelnoulli, a longitudinal model that combines the age-dependent effects of polygenic and monogenic variation on health records, separating how much disease each individual accumulates overall from diseases to which they are prone. Mendelnoulli further allows polygenic and monogenic components to exert different influences on latent disease trajectories. We apply the model to 348 diseases, 36 polygenic scores, and 34 monogenic conditions across three biobanks and provide an atlas of the age-dependent effects of inherited variation on common human diseases. We show that polygenic effects change significantly with age, with Mendelnoulli improving held-out one-year discrimination for all 28 diseases tested compared with a model whose polygenic effects are constant over age (median AUC 0.95 vs 0.92). For individuals with no prior diagnoses, Mendelnoulli identified 8.6 more of every 100 new cases than that model, when each flagged the 5\% at highest risk. For genes with an established disease, Mendelnoulli selected that disease for 27 of 30 genes and ranked it first for 17 (7 expected by chance), and recovered known differences in timing, such as earlier breast cancer effects for BRCA1 than BRCA2 (peak 48 vs 66 years). Mendelnoulli provides a unified model of common and rare genetic influences on disease trajectories across the life course.

papers.abstract_full: Summary:  Background Current psychiatric diagnoses lack biological grounding. Using transdiagnostic psychiatric dimensions derived through data-driven genetic studies with large-scale clinical health records of multiple physiological and clinical outcomes, we can gain new insights into biological similarity and differences between such dimensions, informing nosological discourse. Methods Here, we examined data from 108,182 individuals of European-like ancestry and 13,229 African-like ancestry across two healthcare biobanks. Genetic liabilities of individuals were estimated as polygenic scores for five first-order psychopathology factors (compulsive, thought, neurodevelopmental, substance use, internalizing disorders) and one second-order factor (hierarchical/p-factor). Phenome-wide and laboratory-wide association scans encompassed 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory metrics, meta-analyzed across sites. People with lived experience were involved in the design, preparation, interpretation and reporting of this work. Outcomes We observed robust associations with up to 143 conditions (14 disease categories) for first-order factors and 221 conditions (15 categories) for the hierarchical factor (OR=0.75-1.94). Circulatory, digestive, and respiratory diseases were linked to neurodevelopmental, internalizing, and substance use liabilities. Metabolic conditions were negatively associated with thought and compulsive liabilities but positively associated with the remaining three factors. Laboratory results, particularly lipid and glucose metabolism markers, supported these differential findings. Immune markers also showed differential associations, with C-reactive protein and Complement C4 specifically linked to neurodevelopmental and thought factors, respectively. Similar trends emerged in the smaller African-like ancestry sample. Interpretation Overall, these findings support ongoing efforts to define biologically informed subtypes in psychiatry, such as immuno-metabolic profiles, which can facilitate patient stratification in clinical trials and support transdiagnostic precision psychiatry approaches. papers.abstract_full: Background  Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patients have been little used to model polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, formerly polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS), and differences between unrelated donors can masquerade as disease effects. Earlier comparisons of three or four donors per group reported hundreds to thousands of differentially expressed genes. We asked whether a disease signature is detectable in a larger, genotyped panel, balanced for BMI category and BMI-adjusted, of full-phenotype patients. Methods  We studied 14 clonal, transgene-free iPSC lines reprogrammed by CRISPR activation from endometrial stromal fibroblasts of seven women with PMOS meeting all three Rotterdam criteria, and seven controls frequency-matched for BMI category (30 kg/m²). Bulk RNA-seq (16,489 expressed genes) was related to diagnosis, hormones, metabolic traits, age, and X-inactive specific transcript (XIST) status using gene-wise models, exact enumeration of all 3,432 group splits, and permutation-calibrated gene-set tests. Donors were genotyped within a cohort of 140 women and scored with an imputation-based genome-wide PMOS polygenic risk score (PRS). PMOS risk-locus genes were examined against a 202-line iPSC proteome. Results  PMOS donors had higher anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), testosterone and free androgen index than controls. No gene was differentially expressed between PMOS and control lines (false discovery rate Conclusions  In this panel of 14 undifferentiated iPSC lines from women with the full PMOS phenotype, no robust PMOS-associated transcriptomic differences were detected. Expression variation was dominated by line-to-line differences, consistent with donor background as their main source, although with one clone per donor a contribution of clonal variation cannot be excluded. Reduced XIST expression in some control lines is potentially indicative of, but does not establish, X-chromosome inactivation erosion. Disease-associated differences in differentiated, hormone-responsive cells cannot be excluded, and differences reported in smaller panels may partly reflect inter-donor variability. Future studies should use adequately sized panels, control for XIST erosion, select donors by polygenic risk, and examine hormone-responsive derivatives.

papers.abstract_full: Background and Objectives  Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by demyelination and neuroaxonal injury. Genetics of MS susceptibility and long term disability is well characterized, but the genetic contribution to disability recorded earlier in the disease course is uncertain. We performed common-variant associations with the early period MS severity to identify potential causal loci, effector genes and associated pathways, and understand the relationships of early MS severity and other traits. Methods  The primary outcome was the first age-related MS severity score (ARMSS), an age-adjusted severity measure, in 7,209 individuals of Swedish discovery cohorts and independent Italian and multi-national European replication cohorts. Replicated loci underwent conditional analysis, fine-mapping, time-to-event MS phenotype association analyses, and multi-omics-integrated gene prioritization. Using the genome-wide summary statistics, we also conducted heritability analyses, polygenic risk score association with MS susceptibility and late MS severity, gene-level analyses, cross-trait analyses, Mendelian randomization, and drug-repurposing screening. Results  Two suggestive loci were replicated: rs1234317 on chromosome 1 (effect allele T: beta = 0.100, SE = 0.0189, P = 1.08 × 10  −7 ) and rs929769 on chromosome 5 (effect allele T: beta = −0.0956, SE = 0.0184, P = 1.95 × 10  −7 ). Fine-mapping supported rs929769 strongly in chromosome 5, and rs1234317 and rs6657136 in chromosome 1 with lower confidence. The SNPs did not show a significant change in effect sizes when adjusted for heritable traits and exhibited attenuated associations with long-term MS disability progression.  TNFSF4 was the top prioritized effector for rs1234317,  TNFSF18 for rs6657136, and  ADAMTS2 for rs929769. Early MS severity showed partial genetic overlap with MS susceptibility and late MS severity, but no significant correlation with a range of neurological, psychiatric, autoimmune, cognitive, and aging traits. Pathway analyses identified ion-channel regulation and folic acid metabolism. Mendelian randomization suggested nominal bidirectional causal associations with educational attainment. In silico drug screening nominated several candidate drugs.  Discussion  This study identifies candidate causal variants of early MS severity and their effector genes:  TNFSF4 ,  TNFSF18 , and  ADAMTS2 . It provides insights into the genetic architecture and therapeutic measures for the early phase of MS severity.

Such discordance presents challenges for clinical implementation and return of results (RoR). Methods  We developed a stable PRS for CRC (stPRS-CRC) by integrating 28 published PRS using PRSmix in the All of Us (AoU) development cohort (n=321,703). We investigated spatial G×E for three sequential growth phenotypes, average daily gain before testing (ADGpre), during a 30-day acclimation (ADGacclim) and during the 120-day performance test (ADGtest), in 787 Italian Podolica young bulls from 126 herds in Southern Italy (2001-202…
papers.abstract_full: Genotype-by-environment (G×E) interaction is a key driver of selection efficiency in beef cattle reared across heterogeneous environments, but it has not been quantitatively documented for autochthonous Italian breeds. We investigated spatial G×E for three sequential growth phenotypes, average daily gain before testing (ADGpre), during a 30-day acclimation (ADGacclim) and during the 120-day performance test (ADGtest), in 787 Italian Podolica young bulls from 126 herds in Southern Italy (2001-2022), recorded by the National Association of Italian Beef Cattle Breeders (ANABIC). We derived long-term climatologies of seven biometeorological variables from NASA POWER data across five time windows [late gestation (LG), peri-natal (PERI), neonatal (NEO), mid-suckling (MID), and late-suckling (LATE)] and summarized by window-specific principal components, oriented so that positive values identified hot/dry environments. G×E was tested by likelihood-ratio tests and differences in Akaike's information criterion between nested single-step genomic random-regression animal models (4,382 pedigreed and 1,070 genotyped animals, 21,034 SNPs), analyses were conducted using reaction-norm sire models. The same animal models were fitted in a Bayesian framework to estimate heritability as a function of the environment, h²(ENV). Posterior heritabilities without an environmental covariate were 0.11, 0.26, and 0.31 for ADGpre, ADGacclim and ADGtest. For ADGtest, G×E was not detected in LG and was significant in all four post-natal windows (FDR-corrected p ≤ 0.006), supporting maternal-fetal buffering during gestation. In these windows, heritability of ADGtest was higher in cool/humid (0.43-0.50) than in hot/dry environments (0.24-0.27), with differences whose 95% highest posterior density intervals excluded zero, and additive genetic correlations between environments of 0.48-0.58, suggesting moderate re-ranking of bulls. ADGacclim showed the same direction with less reliable estimates, whereas ADGpre showed the opposite direction, supported only in LG and consistent with confounding by maternal and management effects at the home farm. These results suggest that the genetic determination of Podolica growth varies along the spatial climate gradient of the breed range, with higher expected genetic gain for ADGtest in cool environments, and could lay the foundation for a potential environment-aware genomic evaluation. The Italian Podolica is an ancient cattle breed traditionally reared in the harsh, semi-extensive grazing systems of Southern Italy, from the cold highlands of the Apennines highlands to the warm Mediterranean lowlands. Animals from different farms experience very different climates throughout their early lives, but it is unknown whether these environmental differences affect. Using over twenty years of performance data collected by the Italian Beef Cattle Breeders Association (ANABIC) on nearly eight hundred bulls from one hundred and twenty-six farms, we examined whether the genetic potential for growth depends on the climate of the farm of origin. We combined long-term climate records from the NASA POWER satellite-based database with pedigree information from more than 4000 and DNA data from more than 1000 individuals. Our results show that genetics more strongly determines growth differences in cold, highland environments than in warm, lowland ones, and that the ranking of bulls for growth may partly change between these environments. These findings can help design more accurate genetic evaluation strategies tailored to local climate, supporting sustainable selection of this autochthonous breed in a changing climate.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Unbiased evaluation of liver-derived factors may clarify endocrine links between hepatic metabolism and skeletal fragility; however, hepatic transcript abundance cannot be assumed to represent circulating protein or direct bone-cell signaling. METHODS: We screened 168 liver-secreted genes and 202 independent liver cis-eQTL signals across seven skeletal outcomes using outcome-wise false-discovery-rate control, Steiger direction checks, bilateral sum of single effects (SuSiE) fine-mapping, and a three-edge analysis of liver expression, circulating protein, and heel estimated bone mineral density (eBMD). LEAP2 was then examined in human liver cell-resolved, spatial and bulk datasets, public bone transcriptomes, an exploratory hospital serum cohort [30 osteoporosis (OP) and 30 nonosteoporosis (NOP) participants], and a 2 × 2 high-fat diet (HFD) × orchidectomy (Orx) mouse experiment. RESULTS: The confirmatory genetic screen was null. In the separately defined exploratory layer, LEAP2-heel eBMD was the sole pair meeting the prespecified bilateral SuSiE criteria (PP.H4 = 0.915327); heel eBMD is quantitative-ultrasound-derived rather than a dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) outcome. The MR association remained significant after a post hoc Bonferroni correction across all 1,414 signal-outcome combinations (adjusted p = 1.39 × 10-14). Colocalization was prior-sensitive: PP.H4 was 0.8439 at p 12 = 5 × 10-6 and 0.1903 under a deliberately conservative p 12 = 1 × 10-5/46 stress test, so no formal family-wise colocalization claim was made. The liver eQTL-circulating pQTL edge was analytically indeterminate because the pQTL model did not converge, and the complete genetic triangle was not supported. Hepatocytes dominated LEAP2 signal in all three cell-resolved datasets. Serum LEAP2 was lower in OP than NOP participants (median [IQR], 5.336 [3.780-6.083] vs. 8.153 [7.015-9.458] ng/mL; U = 854, p = 2.33 × 10-9), but age imbalance and unavailable metabolic covariates preclude an independent association claim. In mice, HFD and Orx were associated with adverse trabecular phenotypes and lower hepatic Leap2 and circulating LEAP2. CONCLUSION: A null confirmatory screen and prior-sensitive exploratory colocalization nominate LEAP2 for further study but do not establish circulating mediation, direct bone-cell GHSR signaling, diagnostic utility, or a causal effect on bone.

papers.abstract_full: Long-read sequencing (LRS) and diploid genome assembly have enabled nearly complete structural variant (SV) discovery. Using 293 nearly complete genomes, we characterize the full spectrum of genetic variation and show that while 99% of the variants between any two genomes are single base-pair substitutions, 88% of the euchromatic variant base pairs are SVs, including insertions, deletions, duplications, and inversions. We identify 24 gene-rich regions subject to megabase-scale variation, 2,293 potentially unstable tandem repeats, and 890 novel expression quantitative trait loci associated with SVs in humans. Expanding to 1,218 LRS samples from the 1000 Genomes Project and applying a newly developed cross-platform breakpoint evaluation tool, BoostSV, we construct a nonredundant callset comprising 614,522 SVs. We demonstrate the utility of this population-level SV reference callset by filtering >99% of the common variation from 44 unsolved LRS probands from the Undiagnosed Diseases Network to discover likely disease-causing SVs. Second, we genotype 1,053 high-impact biallelic SVs from the pangenome callset in 232,090 samples from All of Us and discover 105 SVs with significant associations, including 26% where the SV is the lead variant. This publicly available pangenome SV resource will drive new disease associations and further our understanding of the missing heritability of human genetic disease.

Their contribution to pediatric neurological disease remains poorly defined. papers.abstract_full: Pathogenic variants in MT-RNR1 are classically associated with aminoglycoside-induced sensorineural hearing loss through disruption of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA decoding center. Their contribution to pediatric neurological disease remains poorly defined. We identified a novel homoplasmic MT-RNR1 variant, m.1014A>G, in a patient with drug-resistant focal epilepsy beginning at 9 months of age who remained undiagnosed after trio whole-exome sequencing filtered using an extensive epilepsy gene panel. The variant was also detected in her mother. Structural modeling suggests that the variant, affecting a highly conserved region of the mitochondrial 12S rRNA, may alter the mitochondrial small ribosomal subunit assembly. To investigate its pathogenicity, we performed comprehensive functional studies in patient-derived fibroblasts. Unlike canonical MT-RNR1 variants, m.1014A>G did not confer aminoglycoside toxicity. Functional in vitro studies on patients' fibroblasts demonstrated increased 12S/16S rRNA ratios, reduced abundance of both mitoribosomal subunit proteins, decreased levels of mitochondrially encoded respiratory-chain subunits, and impaired oxidative phosphorylation. These abnormalities were accompanied by mitochondrial network fragmentation, increased mitochondria-lysosome colocalization suggestive of enhanced mitophagy and reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number. Altogether, the findings are consistent with defective mitoribosome assembly and altered mitochondrial translation, resulting in a bioenergetic defect. Our study points to a previously unrecognized candidate pathogenic mechanism associated with MT-RNR1 and may expand the phenotypic spectrum of MT-RNR1-related disorders to include maternally inherited infantile-onset epileptic encephalopathy. These findings highlight the importance of dedicated mitochondrial DNA analysis in children with unexplained early-onset epilepsy despite negative nuclear genomic testing.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Background:  Acceleration over the first 20 m is a determining factor in 100 m sprint performance. Elite olympic athletes appear to use individual combinations of spatio-temporal parameters to enhance acceleration performance, but whether this holds for para-athletes and what role different impairments play remains unknown. The aim was to compare performance and spatio-temporal parameters between para- and olympic athletes during the acceleration phase and examine the role of classification group within para-athletes.  Methods:  23 para-athletes (10 female; seven classification groups) and 20 olympic athletes (10 female), highly-trained to world-class, performed maximal 20 m sprints from blocks. Velocity was measured by laser and touchdown events by optical measurement units. Step length to step frequency and contact time to flight time ratios were normalised to biological or artificial leg length, averaged over the steps to 20 m and expressed as z-scores relative to sex-specific olympic athlete values, defining the spatio-temporal signature. Velocity was analysed with a linear mixed model and signatures with permutational multivariate analysis of variance and a nested variance decomposition (athletes within classification groups).  Results:  Para-athletes accelerated more slowly, with a velocity deficit that increased from 0.60 m·s⁻¹ at 5 m to 1.17 m·s⁻¹ at 20 m (cohort × distance, p Conclusion:  Para-athletes showed a progressive velocity deficit but no distinct para-specific spatio-temporal signature. Classification group appeared to constrain spatio-temporal signatures, yet individual variation dominated, suggesting that athletes combine spatio-temporal parameters individually within classification-specific bandwidths. This study outlines a practical tool for profiling spatio-temporal signatures and may support training approaches referenced to an athlete’s own profile rather than group-based norms.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Background  How much of gut fungal abundance is under host genetic control, and whether the same loci contribute to autoimmune liver disease (AILD), is not well mapped. Methods  We used gut mycobiome genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics (N = 7,350) for  Malassezia  ,  Saccharomyces  and  Aspergillus  abundance, and AILD GWAS for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC, N = 24,510), primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC, N = 14,890) and autoimmune hepatitis (AIH, N = 485,234). Gene-based, gene-set and cell-type tests were run in MAGMA/FUMA with Bonferroni correction; colocalization, regional-overlap and cis-eQTL matching linked fungal and AILD loci under a triangulation framework. Results  Host control was genus-specific: the two yeasts carried strong gene-level signal (  Malassezia  85,  Saccharomyces  70 significant genes) with non-overlapping pathway signatures (intracellular processing versus leukocyte recruitment), while  Aspergillus  had none at gene level. On the disease side, PBC returned 381 significant genes and 217 significant gene sets led by adaptive-immunity themes, PSC returned 20 gene sets led by MHC class II antigen presentation, cell-type analysis placed  Malassezia  signals in myeloid and AILD signals in lymphoid compartments; no fungal genus showed gene-level signal in the HLA region. Drug-gene annotation identified SYK (fostamatinib, approved) as the most actionable node of the antifungal-recognition pathway. No fungal-AILD window reached formal colocalization (maximum PP.H4 = 0.16, reflecting limited power). One locus showed single-SNP concordance (chr4:130.2 Mb, C4orf33/SCLT1/PHF17), one strong cis-eQTL support (chr11, AIP cis-eQTL up to |Z| = 15.0), and one regional overlap alone (chr14). AIH yielded no testable window (insufficient variant overlap). Conclusions  Gut fungal abundance exhibits genus-specific host genetic regulation. This first locus-level joint genetic analysis of gut mycobiome and AILD identifies prioritised candidate loci and immune pathways: two prioritised loci (chr4 with single-SNP triangulation, chr11 marked by strong AIP cis-eQTL) and the nominally associated IL-23R immune node; the gene-level structure is robust to ancestry-matched reanalysis, whereas SUMO pathway replication is panel-dependent. These candidates define where fungal and cholangitis genetics meet and are ready for functional follow-up. SYK-fostamatinib is the one annotated axis with an approved drug, untested in AILD; replication in ancestry-matched cohorts is pending.

papers.abstract_full: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are first-line treatments for depression, but response is highly variable, and no robust genetic predictors have been identified. We conducted a genome-wide association meta-analysis of self-reported SSRI response in 62,879 individuals of European ancestry with depression (72.6% responders) across six cohorts (seven datasets), followed by gene-set, transcriptomic, proteomic, drug-target and polygenic score (PGS) analyses. SNP-based heritability was modest but significant (h  2 = 3.1%, SE = 1.4%) with no genome-wide significant variants detected. Gene-set analyses implicated gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)ergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission, and a gene involved in glutamate transport (  SLC17A6 ) showed consistent sub-threshold evidence across pathway, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses. Drug-target enrichment for hypnotics, anxiolytics and general anesthetics further supported the GABAergic signal. A leave-one-out PGS from the discovery meta-analysis was associated with self-reported SSRI response in independent cohorts (meta-analysis OR = 1.05, 95% CI 1.02—1.08, p = 0.002). Higher PGS for depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), autism, addiction and schizophrenia were associated with lower odds of reported SSRI response, with ADHD, PTSD, autism and addiction remaining after adjustment for depression PGS. In contrast, educational attainment PGS was associated with better SSRI response. Self-reported SSRI response captures genetic insights relevant to antidepressant response, implicating GABAergic and glutamatergic neurotransmission. Individuals with higher genetic loading for psychiatric conditions report poorer response, and higher genetic loading for educational attainment PGS a better reported response. Although larger studies are needed to identify specific variants, self-report offers a practical, patient-centered and scalable route to collect the larger samples required.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  Atrophic gastritis (AG), characterized by chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa and glandular atrophy, is an established precursor of gastric cancer (GC) and contributes to iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia. Although Helicobacter pylori infection is a major environmental determinant, not all infected individuals develop AG or GC, suggesting that host genetic factors influence susceptibility to AG and severe atrophic gastritis (SAG). Previous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of AG have been limited in size and have not adequately compared anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus strata, leaving potential genetic heterogeneity unresolved.  Methods We performed GWAS meta-analyses of AG and SAG, stratified by anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus, involving 214,747 Japanese participants: 75,074 in the discovery phase and 139,673 in the replication phase. Subsequent analyses included genotype-by-serostatus interactions, HLA allele and ABO blood group associations, genome-wide genetic correlations, multi-trait analysis, local genetic correlations, and structural equation modeling. In addition, cross-ancestry meta-analyses were performed using chronic gastritis GWAS data from FinnGen, UK Biobank, and the Million Veteran Program, comprising 1,357,053 participants.  Results Across six Japanese GWAS meta-analyses, we identified genome-wide significant associations at 17 genomic regions. Strong associations with seropositive AG/SAG were observed at previously reported GC susceptibility loci, including PSCA and MUC1/MTX1, whereas the MHC class II region showed predominant associations with seronegative AG/SAG. FAP, CCR6, and ATP4A were also found to be associated with seronegative SAG. The identified regions included previously reported GC susceptibility regions MUC1/MTX1, PRKAA1/PTGER4, PSCA, ABO, and MHC. Associations at PSCA and MUC1/MTX1 were replicated at a genome-wide significance level, supporting a shared genetic basis between AG/SAG and GC. Additional AG-associated candidate regions included BMP2, CCDC80, LRRC34, CPEB4, PGC/FRS3, and LMTK2, implicating epithelial regulation, immune responses, transcriptional regulation, and differentiation. A positive genotype-by-serostatus interaction for SAG was observed at MUC1/MTX1. HLA class II alleles, including HLA-DRB1*15:01 and HLA-DQB1*06:02, showed associations with seronegative AG/SAG. The LDSC genetic correlation between AG and GC was 0.529, and the MTAG estimated Omega correlation was 0.694. Local genetic correlation analysis and structural equation modeling further supported shared genetic components. Cross-ancestry integration of seronegative SAG with external chronic gastritis GWAS data identified an additional association at TPTEP1.  Conclusions Our findings characterize the genetic heterogeneity of serologically defined AG/SAG according to anti-H. pylori IgG serostatus. They highlight epithelial and mucus barrier-related pathways in seropositive AG/SAG and immune-related pathways in seronegative cases, while also providing evidence of a shared genetic basis between AG and GC. Together, these results clarify the genetic basis of a GC precursor and are consistent with a continuum from chronic inflammation through atrophy to carcinogenesis. These insights may inform prevention strategies and personalized management of the diverse health consequences of AG.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Asthma disproportionately affects African ancestry populations, yet its genetic architecture remains poorly characterized due to persistent underrepresentation in genomic studies. We integrated genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for asthma and white blood cell traits in African ancestry cohorts. Genome-wide and local genetic correlations were assessed using linkage disequilibrium score regression, and cross-trait associations were identified using a conditional false discovery rate framework. We identified a robust positive genetic correlation between asthma and eosinophil counts, together with several ancestry-specific local signals. Cross-trait analysis identified 78 novel pleiotropic loci, including an African-specific locus upstream of CD36, complementing evidence from East Asian populations. We also identified an African-specific association at CD226 (rs8087187), independent of previously reported European associations. Flow cytometry in 19 patients with asthma and 19 healthy controls demonstrated increased CD226 expression in CD4⁺ T cells from patients with asthma, supporting its functional relevance. Our findings reveal ancestry-specific genetic and immune mechanisms underlying asthma and highlight the importance of diverse populations in elucidating the genetic architecture of complex diseases.

papers.abstract_full: Genome-wide association studies of the metabolome have predominantly examined European-ancestry populations using a single biofluid, constraining both the discovery of metabolite quantitative trait loci (mQTLs) and the resolution of causal variant finemapping. Here, we report a multi-ancestry genome-wide association study of 1,955 serum and urine metabolites in 4,431 European American and African American participants from the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study. We identify 969 mQTLs for 553 metabolites, 30% unreported in studies of matched biofluid and ancestry, and replicate 91-99% of testable mQTLs in two independent cohorts. In the African American sample with balanced sample sizes, 36% of metabolites with mQTLs are serum-specific, 39% urine-specific, and 25% shared, demonstrating complementary genetic architecture. Only 23 of 632 candidate ancestry-specific mQTLs show heterogeneous effects beyond variant availability and power, yet allele frequency differences expose functional variants such as an  SLC28A1 splice variant, virtually absent in Europeans, that increases urine uridine excretion, implicating impaired CNT1-mediated renal nucleoside reabsorption. Multi-ancestry finemapping improves credible set resolution, and colocalization with the Million Veteran Program phenome links the catalog to cardiometabolic, kidney and liver traits consistent with prioritized gene function. Integrating biofluids and ancestries enhances genetic discovery and mechanistic characterization of the human metabolome.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Background:  Breast cancer incidence has continued to rise over recent decades. Beyond established genetic and hormonal factors, neuropsychiatric conditions including depression, anxiety, and sleep disturbances, have emerged as independent risk factors. Brain structure, as a core neuroendocrine substrate, may share genetic determinants with breast cancer risk; however, this relationship remains insufficiently characterized.  Objective:  This study investigated the potential genetic correlations between brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) and breast cancer using genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics via Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis. We hypothesized that shared genetic architecture between neuropsychiatric traits and breast cancer may reveal previously unrecognized biological pathways.  Methods:  We conducted MR analysis to systematically evaluate potential causal associations between 4,013 IDPs and 14 breast cancer (BC) traits, encompassing overall BC and molecular subtypes. Genetic instruments for IDPs were obtained from the UK Biobank and ENIGMA consortium. Summary-level BC data were sourced from IEU OpenGWAS, FinnGen, and the GWAS Catalog, covering European and African ancestry populations. A combined multi-ancestry linkage disequilibrium (LD) reference panel was constructed to optimize instrument clumping. The inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method served as the primary analysis, supported by sensitivity tests and colocalization to assess robustness and identify shared causal loci.  Results:  Temporal lobe structure demonstrated the strongest causal associations with estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer. Within this region, the fusiform gyrus showed the most consistent negative causal effects across European ancestry datasets: right fusiform volume (IDP: GCST90002807,  P  -value = 2.23×10  -7  ), right fusiform surface area (IDP: GCST90003180,  P  -value = 1.11×10  -6  ), and left fusiform surface area (IDP: GCST90003079,  P  -value = 5.23×10  -6  ). Cross-ancestry analyses highlighted substantial population heterogeneity, as associations identified in European cohorts were not replicated in African ancestry datasets. Colocalization further localized shared genetic signals to chromosomes 17 and 12, implicating genes such as  ARL17B  and  NSFP1  , which are enriched in pathways related to intracellular vesicular transport and membrane dynamics.  Conclusion:  Our findings reveal a causal relationship between brain structure and breast cancer risk, identifying the fusiform gyrus as a key region associated with ER+ BC. The study uncovers a shared genetic basis underlying this brain-breast axis, centered on genes involved in vesicular transport and membrane regulation. These insights suggest that neural processes may contribute to cancer susceptibility and provide new directions for biomarker development and mechanistic research.

papers.abstract_full: Non-human primates are an ideal model for interrogating the genetic basis of human lifespan and resilience due to their long lifespan compared to other model organisms, development of similar age-related chronic conditions, and genetic similarity. However, like humans, statistical methods for modeling survival suffer from the challenges of dealing with non-proportionality of hazards, large numbers of living individuals that must be censored, and loss-to-follow-up over studies that may last a decade or more. Here we overcome these challenges through the use of pseudo-observations of Restricted Mean Survival Time as a measure of resilience to the acute challenge of radiation exposure and chronic challenges of aging and a Western-style diet in rhesus macaques (  Macaca mulatta ) from the Wake Forest Non-Human Primate Radiation Late Effects Cohort. Our whole-exome analysis used Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) to identify variants associated with longevity, and a subsequent Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted the cadherin and integrin signaling pathways as central to this resilience. As dysregulation of cell adhesion and extracellular matrix signaling is central to the development of fibrosis, we tested the functional relevance of these signals using a targeted Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) score-weighted Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal (SKAT-O) analysis of GSEA leading-edge genes from both the cadherin and integrin pathways. This linked variant burden in  PCDHGA5, PCDHGA3, PCDHGB2, PCDHA11, and  PSENEN to the severity of myocardial fibrosis, and in  IBSP, PDGFD, and  LAMC2 to the severity of pulmonary fibrosis observed at necropsy. Critically, we note that the genetic variants are not caused by the radiation but rather create an underlying risk for disease that is then exacerbated by the acute and persistent stressors challenging these animals’ intrinsic resilience. The success of this method in identifying biologically relevant genetic variants underlying survival in animals undergoing a strong challenge to their resilience highlights not only the role of genes predisposing animals to fibrosis in lifespan, but the overall utility of pseudo-observations in overcoming the limitations of survival analyses in humans and other long-lived species.

papers.abstract: Polygenic prediction of depression is limited by the depth of depression phenotyping available at biobank scale as well as sample size. papers.abstract_full: Polygenic prediction of depression is limited by the depth of depression phenotyping available at biobank scale as well as sample size. Here we develop a depression score combining information from depression and genetically correlated psychiatric traits using phenotype reconstruction, multi-trait genetic integration and Bayesian effect estimation. Compared with the strongest publicly available depression-only score (Psychiatric Genomics Consortium 2025, excluding 23andMe), the liability-  R 2 for depression in UK Biobank rose by 49.7% and within-family standardized associations with latent internalizing were up to 54% larger. Across 2,328 childhood and adolescent outcomes in the ABCD study, the association profile of the integrated score was almost identical to that of the depression-only score (r = 0.99), while being uniformly stronger. 1,494 outcomes related to mood, behavior, social functioning, hobbies and sleep were associated with the score — 423 of them within-family. In ABCD, adolescents in the highest score decile were 3.5 times as likely as those in the lowest decile to report suicidal thoughts by age 14 (23% versus 7%) and 1.9 times as likely to report nicotine or cannabis use by age 17 (47% versus 25%). In adults, the score predicted worse general health, chronic pain, and life dissatisfaction. Associations with psychiatric symptoms were substantially stronger in girls than in boys (boys’ coeffiicients 0.68 times girls’), particularly for girl-typical symptoms, and showed no moderation by household resources, hardship or deprivation that remained significant after correction for multiple testing. Prediction was attenuated in line with genetic distance from training data for Hispanic and African American children. Depression prediction can thus be strengthened substantially by integrating the internalizing spectrum, without detectable loss of specificity or within-family predictive ability.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) has substantial heritability. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) often use single-nucleotide polygenic risk scores to estimate this inherited risk, but macro-scale structural alterations remain under-explored. We evaluated whether chromosome-level structural variation (CLSV) provides a predictive signal for AMI. We quantified this variation as statistical moments of microarray Log R Ratio (LRR) distributions across 128 segments of the genome. We performed 1:1 matching between cases and controls on sex at birth, self-reported race, and age (\(\:\le\:\pm\:2\) years) within the  All of Us  Research Program Controlled Tier dataset (\(\:N=3,290\)) to eliminate demographic confounding. We evaluated Random Forest models across 10 independent stratified cross-validation splits. The CLSV model achieved a 10-split mean held-out test ROC AUC of  0.529  (SD: \(\:0.048\), 10-split range: \(\:0.439\) to \(\:0.604\)). This performance is statistically indistinguishable from a scrambled target control (\(\:0.491\), 10-split range: \(\:0.465\) to \(\:0.546\)) and overlaps random chance (\(\:0.500\)). A positive biological control predicting sex at birth using the same genomic moment extraction pipeline achieved near-perfect discrimination (mean AUC = \(\:0.999\), 10-split range: \(\:0.997\) to \(\:1.000\)), confirming high technical validity. We establish with 95% statistical confidence that any true predictive signal carried by broad structural genomic variation in an unconfounded matched cohort is less than an upper 95% confidence limit of 0.585 (Nadeau–Bengio corrected, mean AUC = 0.529). Our findings suggest that macro-scale structural variation does not explain missing heritability or provide clinical risk discrimination for AMI.

papers.title: Between promise and guidance: a systematic review of normative documents on polygenic risk scores in healthcare contexts.
papers.abstract: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) have shown increasing predictive value for several common complex diseases and generated expectations regarding their potential clinical and public health applications. papers.abstract_full: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) have shown increasing predictive value for several common complex diseases and generated expectations regarding their potential clinical and public health applications. Despite growing research and translational initiatives, PRS have yet to be integrated into routine clinical practice. The limited uptake of PRS has been linked to scientific limitations and a lack of clear guidance. More recently, the emergence of professional and policy documents addressing PRS points to an evolving normative landscape that warrants careful consideration. To this end, we conducted a systematic review of normative documents addressing the prospective use of PRS in healthcare contexts, including clinical guidelines, consensus statements, and policy reports issued by professional societies, regulatory bodies, and healthcare institutions. Searches were conducted across major biomedical and policy databases, complemented by grey literature sources and targeted website searches. Twenty-six documents met the inclusion criteria. None explicitly endorsed the routine implementation of PRS in healthcare at present. Most adopted cautious positions, citing limited evidence of clinical utility, concerns about transferability, and ethical risks. Substantial variation was observed in scope and degree of prescriptivity. While broad agreement existed on general best practices-such as defining test purpose, integrating PRS with other risk factors, and ensuring appropriate counsel​ing-guidance was often non-prescriptive, leaving key implementation thresholds and value commitments implicit. The findings highlight an emerging but fragmented normative landscape in which guidance has not yet globally translated into clear, action-guiding standards for clinical practice and implementation in healthcare. Clarifying how evidence, value commitments, and responsibilities translate into statements is essential to inform ongoing and future deliberations on the responsible use and implementation of PRS.

papers.abstract: As genomics has entered the 'big data' era over the past 2 decades, phenotypic prediction has become central to fields ranging from livestock production to human health. papers.abstract_full: As genomics has entered the 'big data' era over the past 2 decades, phenotypic prediction has become central to fields ranging from livestock production to human health. In the latest case, efforts have focused primarily on the development of polygenic risk scores (PRS), derived from genome-wide association (GWA) studies. As prediction methods gained popularity, earlier gene-mapping approaches have been largely perceived as a dead end. Gene-mapping experiments did not rapidly reach the high level of expectation they raised, and the incentives for further improving their methodologies soon decreased. It could be argued that the study of genotype-phenotype relationships has taken sides in the broader scientific debate between prediction and explanation (also referred as causation or understanding). But fortunately, a major obstacle to the search of complex, polygenic (or even more broadly, polyfactorial) bases of traits has recently been overcome. Technically, the Natural and Orthogonal InterActions (NOIA) model enables unbiased estimates of effects of complex genetic and environmental architectures of traits, even in datasets with severe departures from equilibrium genotypic frequencies. This achievement significantly increases our potential to reveal the factors underlying phenotypes and allows for a sounder interpretation and reliable comparisons of different mapping experiments on the same trait. Improving our understanding of the relationship among genes, environments, and traits may provide us with countless advantages. Thus, the potential of advanced genetic modeling for studying complex traits needs to be assessed in practice, particularly when evidence suggests that PRS may be approaching a structural limit.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: The diagnosis of pneumonia in children based on clinical findings is challenging. The Pneumonia Risk Score (PRS), a clinical prediction tool, estimates the risk of radiographic pneumonia. Most children are classified as moderate-risk and are recommended to undergo chest x-ray (CXR). We hypothesized that lung ultrasound (LUS) may add diagnostic value beyond the PRS for predicting radiographic pneumonia. METHODS: We studied a convenience sample of children 6 months to 18 years old enrolled in a prospective LUS registry who presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory complaints and underwent CXR and LUS. The primary outcome was radiographic pneumonia. Logistic regression included the five PRS clinical predictors, and LUS consolidation ≥1 cm with bronchograms was added to create the PRS + LUS model. We compared the area under the curve (AUC) of the PRS to the PRS + LUS, evaluated risk re-classifications, and proposed a novel diagnostic algorithm. RESULTS: Among 275 children, 58 (21%) had radiographic pneumonia. LUS consolidation was strongly associated with pneumonia (OR 28.68 [95% CI, 9.98 to 82.43]). The PRS + LUS demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy than the PRS alone (AUC 0.85 [95% CI, 0.77 to 0.89] versus 0.70 [95% CI, 0.61 to 0.76]; P < 0.001). Using our proposed novel two-step diagnostic algorithm, the PRS + LUS was calculated for patients assigned a moderate-risk score by PRS, resulting in assigning an additional 120 (44%) patients a high- or low-risk score, decreasing the moderate-risk category. CONCLUSION: Adding LUS to the PRS improves prediction of radiographic pneumonia and may reduce CXR use, particularly among patients with moderate risk.

papers.abstract_full: In low-input proteomics, proteome coverage is often limited not only by sample amount but also by inefficient tandem mass spectrometry (MS) sampling of peptide-rich acquisition space. During capillary electrophoresis (CE)-electrospray ionization (ESI)-MS analysis, electrophoretically separated peptides occupy reproducible, correlated regions of migration time, precursor mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), and ion mobility (IM), creating an opportunity to direct data-independent acquisition (DIA) toward peptide-enriched regions. Here, we introduce electrophoresis-correlative diaPASEF (Eco-diaPASEF), a CE-informed implementation of diaPASEF that uses migration time-correlated m/z and IM information to define complementary acquisition segments while maintaining the reference cycle time. By restricting IM scan range, precursor m/z space, and DIA isolation width, Eco-diaPASEF focuses tandem MS acquisition on peptide-enriched regions. In low-input HeLa digest samples, Eco-diaPASEF increased protein-group (PG) identifications by up to ∼65% relative to conventional diaPASEF, cumulatively identifying up to 1163 PGs across 4 technical replicates from 200 pg of digest measured per run on a timsTOF Pro mass spectrometer. Applied to single animal-cap cells from stage-9 Xenopus laevis embryos, Eco-diaPASEF cumulatively quantified 1108 PGs across 3 cells using ∼200 pg of injected digest per cell. The method provided ∼2.6-2.7-fold greater proteome coverage across replicate criteria while maintaining comparable biological-replicate precision. These results establish Eco-diaPASEF as a CE-guided acquisition strategy for improving proteome coverage in low-input and single-cell CE-ESI-MS proteomics on IM-enabled mass spectrometers.

papers.abstract_full: Multifactorial genetic diseases (as currently applicable for incompletely understood genetic conditions such as lipedema) present a polygenic architecture in which numerous common Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) contribute to overall risk with small summed effects. Traditional Polygenic Risk Scores (PRS) rely on GWAS-derived effect sizes, which are often unavailable or poorly transferable for understudied or rare diseases. This study proposes a summary-statistics-independent (external-GWAS-independent) pipeline for PRS construction and illustrates its application in lipedema. Our pipeline uses individual-level data (n=314; 208 cases, 106 controls) and preselected variants chosen based on biological relevance and physio-logical pathways involved. A standardized workflow includes quality control, alignment, variant calling, annotation, and genotype filtering. A linear Support Vector Machine (SVM) ranks variants by absolute weight to identify the most informative features. Ridge regression with L2 regularization is then applied to derive stable PRS weights. Model performance is evaluated using AUC, accuracy, F1 score, and Nagelkerke's pseudo-R². Analyses of PRS distributions and predictor importance emphasize interpretability and capture weak but cumulative signals. The model achieved an AUC of 0.87 and a Nagelkerke's pseudo-R² of 0.13, indicating meaningful capture of aggregated genetic risk. The proposed summary-statistics-independent pipeline offers a transparent and clinically interpretable strategy for PRS development in GWAS-scarce multifactorial diseases. The combined SVM-ridge strategy appears robust and 140 adaptable, with encouraging performance in lipedema and potential for translational risk stratification. These results should be considered proof-of-concept, pending external validation.

papers.abstract_full: Polygenic associations with neurodevelopmental traits may reflect both direct and indirect genetic effects. However, evidence separating these effects is limited and mixed, and rarely spans development or reporters, or triangulates across methods. We triangulated twin-comparison and trio-based analyses in the Twins Early Development Study, using eight polygenic scores (PGS) and repeated parent, teacher and self-reports of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) traits from ages 4 to 26. Analyses included up to 7,259 offspring with observed or imputed parental genetic data. Both approaches consistently supported direct genetic effects of ADHD and ASD PGS on corresponding traits, whereas evidence for within-trait indirect effects was limited. Cross-trait indirect effects emerged for several PGS, particularly in parent reports, and some were unexpectedly negative. These findings suggest that within-trait polygenic prediction of ADHD and ASD traits mainly reflects direct rather than indirect genetic effects, whereas cross-trait associations reflect some indirect genetic effects.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Network analysis is a popular method for assessing the comorbidity of psychiatric symptoms. Studies have reported inconsistent group differences in symptom networks based on risk factors such as sex and trauma exposure. We conducted the most comprehensive study of group differences in symptom networks to date, analysing nine depression, six anxiety, and three PTSD symptoms in the UK Biobank (N=130,519). We tested group differences based on four polygenic scores and eight demographic/environmental risk factors, using thirteen network comparison metrics. Feelings of worthlessness were the leading bridge symptom, suggesting a central role in explaining or predicting comorbidity. We found significant group differences for eleven risk factors, with sex and childhood trauma showing the broadest patterns. Group differences were greater for symptom relationships within than across conditions. We find broad associations between risk factors and networks of internalising symptoms, which may help foster greater understanding of psychiatric risk and group specific interventions.

papers.abstract: Background:  /Objectives: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) combine many genetic variants to estimate disease risk. Their clinical value depends on whether the information improves preventive decisions and patient outcomes. This critical evidence review examines selected clinical, implementation, qualitative, prediction and economic studies relevant to adult primary care. Methods: Evidence was identified through public-web searches, citation tracking and executed PubMed/MEDLINE and CENTRAL searches, t…
papers.abstract_full: Background:  /Objectives: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) combine many genetic variants to estimate disease risk. Their clinical value depends on whether the information improves preventive decisions and patient outcomes. This critical evidence review examines selected clinical, implementation, qualitative, prediction and economic studies relevant to adult primary care. Methods: Evidence was identified through public-web searches, citation tracking and executed PubMed/MEDLINE and CENTRAL searches, then selected for its relevance to preventive care. Findings were organized by clinical decision, study design and outcome, with GRADE profiles for 14 comparisons within the assessed evidence. Results: Risk disclosure linked to a shared statin decision may increase treatment initiation and lower LDL cholesterol, although its long-term cardiovascular benefit remains very uncertain. Several information programmes showed limited short-term effects on objectively measured behaviour or weight. An integrated breast-screening programme met its prespecified advanced-cancer noninferiority margin; the contribution of PRS and an effect on biopsy burden remained uncertain. Genetic subgroup analyses address whether treatment effects vary with genetic risk, a different question from whether PRS-guided care improves outcomes. Implementation studies highlight communication, workflow and access needs, while economic models depend on uptake, treatment and cost assumptions. Conclusions: The central clinical distinction is between improved prediction, changed recommendations, care received and better health. Evidence supports selected preventive decision effects and a care-pathway approach to evaluating PRS. Broader implementation requires convincing evidence of patient-important benefit, acceptable downstream harms and equitable access.

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Neural epidermal growth factor-like 1 (NELL1) is a novel antigen in membranous nephropathy (MN). Our observations indicate that a subset of patients with NELL1-associated MN demonstrate focal positive NELL1 and IgG deposition along the tubular basement membrane (TBM), a phenomenon that has been infrequently documented in previous studies. This study aims to validate and elucidate its clinical significance. METHODS: We identified 23 patients with biopsy-confirmed NELL1-associated MN between January 2019 and December 2023. Based on NELL1 staining along the TBM, patients were categorized into TBM-positive (n = 12) and TBM-negative (n = 11) groups. Immunofluorescence dual-labeling was performed to assess the colocalization of NELL1 with IgG and nephron segment-specific tubular markers. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, histopathological, and follow-up data were compared. RESULTS: Immunofluorescence dual-labeling confirmed the colocalization of NELL1 and IgG along the TBM in the TBM-positive group. NELL1 deposition along the TBM was observed in subsets of both thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter- and sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter 2 -positive tubules. Compared with the TBM-negative group, patients in the TBM-positive group were older, exhibited higher proteinuria levels, had impaired renal function, and showed significantly elevated serum anti-NELL1 antibody levels. Furthermore, these patients required a longer time to achieve significant proteinuria remission (24-hour proteinuria < 500 mg). CONCLUSION: NELL1-associated immune deposits along the TBM are observed in a subset of patients with NELL1-associated MN and correlate with higher serum anti-NELL1 antibody levels and more severe clinical features.

Drugs with genetic support from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have substantially greater odds of success, but how best to use GWAS to prioritize drug targets remains unclear. We evaluated the performance of GWAS causal gene prioritization methods from the Open Targets consortium by cross-referencing their predictions with drug trial outcomes for 445 diseases. papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Neurosurgical management of brain tumour patients includes the prompt recognition and individualized treatment of sodium disorders to optimize recovery. The study aimed to assess the effect of serum sodium within 24 hours after brain tumour surgery on clinical outcomes. METHODS: Prospective study of 117 patients undergoing brain tumour surgery. The worst serum sodium value within 24 hours after surgery was recorded. Primary outcome was composite hospital mortality and readmission to the ICU. A generalized linear mixed model was used to assess the effect of serum sodium on the primary outcome. RESULTS: Neurosurgical procedures were supratentorial craniotomy (52.1%), infratentorial craniotomy (29.9%), and endoscopic endonasal surgery (17.9%). Hyperosmolar therapy was associated with higher serum sodium (p = 0.001). Serum sodium was significantly lower in patients with neurological complications than in those without complications (p = 0.008). In the quadratic regression model, serum sodium revealed a U-shaped relationship with ICU length of stay (p < 0.0001; adjusted R2 = 0.680) and a Ո-shaped relationship with FOUR score (p < 0.0001; adjusted R2 = 0.782). The primary outcome occurred in 23 patients (19.7%). Serum sodium had a nonlinear relationship with the primary outcome (p = 0.014) in the multivariate generalized linear mixed model, with an inflexion point at 142.7 mmol/L. CONCLUSIONS: Serum sodium within 24 hours is associated with worse postoperative clinical outcomes and could be used as prognostic biomarker for patients after brain tumour surgery, but further prospective studies are warranted to confirm these results.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Food allergy (FA) is a common immune-mediated disorder, yet its genetic architecture and underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to characterize the genetic architecture of FA, refine association signals through multi-ancestry fine-mapping, and investigate shared genetic and regulatory mechanisms linking FA with asthma and atopic dermatitis (AD). METHODS: We performed a multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis of FA including more than 16,000 cases and over 1 million controls of European, African, and East Asian ancestry. We used sequential conditional analysis and Bayesian fine-mapping to identify independent association signals and prioritize candidate causal variants. We further evaluated shared genetic architecture with asthma and AD through conditional colocalization analysis and integrated FA-associated variants with cis-eQTL and single-nucleus ATAC/RNA-seq data from blood and skin to nominate candidate target genes and disease-relevant cell types. RESULTS: This trans-ancestry design enabled fine-mapping of the 5q31.1 locus (IL4, IL5, and IL13), revealing multiple independent disease-associated signals, including a secondary genome-wide significant variant (rs6873732; p ≤ 5 × 10-8) and a tertiary signal surpassing Bonferroni significance (rs4608913; p = 9.1 × 10-6). Bayesian fine-mapping identified credible causal variants that also associate with asthma and atopic dermatitis (AD). At 5q31.1, three variants within the primary credible set overlapped accessible chromatin in basophils and T cells, while seven tertiary-signal variants overlapped open chromatin in basophils, monocytes, keratinocytes, and CD8+ T cells. Integration with cis-eQTL data demonstrated that primary and tertiary FA signals were associated with increased SLC22A5/IL13 expression and upregulation of IRF1, respectively. CONCLUSION: Together, these findings refine the genetic architecture of FA, reveal shared and disease-specific mechanisms with related allergic diseases, highlight the value of integrating ancestry-diverse GWAS with multi-omics data to prioritize regulatory mechanisms in complex immune-mediated conditions.

papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE: To evaluate the association between diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), corneal sensitivity, and tear matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP-9) with macular microcirculatory parameters assessed by optical coherence tomography angiography (OCT-A) in patients with diabetes mellitus. METHODS: This cross-sectional observational study included 158 eyes of 79 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) undergoing routine retinopathy screening at a single tertiary centre. Superficial capillary plexus vessel density and foveal avascular zone (FAZ) parameters (area, perimeter, and circularity index) were obtained by OCT-A (Cirrus 6000, AngioPlex®, Carl Zeiss Meditec). Corneal sensitivity was measured with the Brill esthesiometer and tear MMP-9 was assessed with the InflammaDry test. DPN was confirmed by electroneuromyography. Linear mixed models with random intercept per patient were applied to account for bilateral data. RESULTS: Among OCT-A parameters, vessel density and FAZ area and perimeter did not show significant association with DPN status, MMP-9 positivity, or corneal sensitivity. FAZ circularity showed a significant negative association with DPN in the multivariable model (β = -0.07; p = 0.021) and with corneal sensitivity in the linear mixed model (β = 0.01; p = 0.049), but was not associated with MMP-9 status (p = 0.691). No OCT-A parameter was associated with MMP-9 in any analysis. CONCLUSIONS: FAZ circularity was independently associated with DPN and with reduced corneal sensitivity, suggesting a potential retinal correlate of neurovascular damage in diabetes; however, this is a model-dependent, exploratory finding requiring prospective confirmation. No OCT-A parameter was associated with MMP-9 status, suggesting compartmental dissociation between anterior segment inflammation and posterior segment microvascular status at this disease stage.

papers.abstract: Stem architecture is a key determinant of lodging resistance, yield potential, and mechanical harvestability in Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum), yet the genetic basis of stem-related traits remains poorly understood. In this study, a diverse panel of 244 Tartary buckwheat accessions was evaluated for five stem architectural traits, including plant height (PH), stem diameter (SD), branch number on the main stem (BNMS), node number on the main stem (NNMS), and stem wall thickness (TST), ac…
papers.abstract_full: Stem architecture is a key determinant of lodging resistance, yield potential, and mechanical harvestability in Tartary buckwheat (Fagopyrum tataricum), yet the genetic basis of stem-related traits remains poorly understood. In this study, a diverse panel of 244 Tartary buckwheat accessions was evaluated for five stem architectural traits, including plant height (PH), stem diameter (SD), branch number on the main stem (BNMS), node number on the main stem (NNMS), and stem wall thickness (TST), across three field environments (Huize 2025, Songming 2024, and Songming 2025). Genome-wide association study (GWAS) was performed using 280,377 high-quality Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) to identify loci associated with stem architecture traits. Substantial phenotypic variation was observed for all traits, with broad-sense heritability varying among traits and environments, likely reflecting the high sensitivity of Tartary buckwheat to environmental conditions across the three contrasting field environments. Strong positive correlations were detected between PH and NNMS, while SD and TST showed weak correlations with other traits, indicating partially independent genetic control. GWAS identified a major significant association region on chromosome (Chr) 4 affecting both PH and NNMS (Chr4: 31011474-31099420), while BNMS, SD, and TST displayed more dispersed or polygenic genetic architectures. Candidate genes within associated regions were mainly annotated to functions related to cell-wall modification, developmental regulation, and metabolic processes, suggesting potential mechanisms underlying stem architecture variation. Cross-trait analysis revealed extensive shared genetic control between PH and NNMS but relatively independent genetic regulation of BNMS and stem mechanical traits. These findings provide novel insights into the genetic architecture of stem traits in Tartary buckwheat and identify candidate loci for marker-assisted breeding of optimized plant architecture. Because PH and NNMS on the one hand and BNMS, SD and TST on the other are under largely independent genetic control, the Chr4 block and the trait-specific loci identified here can be combined by marker-assisted pyramiding to develop lodging-resistant, mechanization-ready cultivars.

papers.abstract_full: Flavonoids are important nutritional components, and total flavonoid content (TFC) is a critical quality trait in peanut (Arachis hypogaea L.) kernels. Identifying the genetic loci and candidate genes underlying TFC is essential for improving nutritional quality through molecular breeding. In this study, quantitative trait locus (QTL) mapping and genome-wide association study (GWAS) were integrated to explore the key loci of TFC in peanut. In a recombinant inbred line (RIL) population evaluated across four environments, TFC ranged from 46.96 to 131.15 mg rutin equivalents (RE)/100 g. A total of 11 QTLs associated with TFC were identified, among which qflvA03.1 and qflvA10.2 were major-effect loci, accounting for 16.95% and 11.64% of the phenotypic variation explained (PVE), respectively. In a natural population of 103 peanut accessions evaluated across three environments, TFC ranged from 63.49 to 129.27 mg RE/100 g. GWAS identified 92 significantly associated single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), explaining 9.15%-18.19% of the phenotypic variation. Four SNPs were co-localized with QTL intervals detected in the RIL population, distributed on chromosomes A06, A10, and B09, contributing 6.60%-8.9% to the PVE. Within 160 kb (r2 = 0.2) regions surrounding these co-localized SNPs, 33 candidate genes potentially involved in flavonoid biosynthesis were identified, including genes encoding 4-coumarate-CoA ligase, isoflavone reductase, anthocyanin 5-aromatic acyltransferase, and flavonol synthase. A Kompetitive Allele-Specific PCR marker was developed at locus A03_124522117. The KASP marker was developed from the qflvA03.1 QTL, and used to validate the association between genotype and flavonoid content. The genotypes carrying CC had significantly higher flavonoid content than those carrying TT. These findings provide insights into the genetic mechanisms underlying TFC in peanuts and establish a foundation for molecular breeding of high-quality, flavonoid-rich peanut varieties.

papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Adnexal torsion is a gynaecological emergency in which ovarian preservation or removal is decided intraoperatively. Prepubertal girls have the longest reproductive and endocrine horizon, yet they are commonly pooled with postmenarchal adolescents. This review estimated how often torsion episodes in prepubertal and prepubertal-predominant paediatric cohorts are managed by oophorectomy, together with imaging findings after ovarian-sparing surgery, recurrence and diagnosed malignancy. Methods: A PRISMA 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD420261496245) searched Europe PMC (including MEDLINE), OpenAlex, preprint servers, ClinicalTrials.gov and citation networks to 2 September 2026, with an update search to 12 October 2026; Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL and CENTRAL were not searched. Eligible cohorts documented premenarchal status (direct evidence) or had a central age of 12.0 years or younger (indirect evidence). Proportions were pooled with a binomial-normal generalised linear mixed model; JBI appraisal and GRADE were applied. Results: Thirty studies were included. Across 14 cohorts (1011 episodes), 42.8% (95% CI 28.1-58.9) were managed by oophorectomy, with extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 94.0%; 95% prediction interval 6.0-89.9%); the estimate was 33.4% (8.5-69.8) in the 4 cohorts with documented premenarchal status and 24.8% (14.4-37.3) in the 7 cohorts meeting all appraisal items. Follicular activity or normal morphology was seen on follow-up imaging in 89.9% (81.9-95.9) of 234 imaged adnexa after ovarian-sparing surgery. Recurrence was 12.9% (6.6-21.0; 11 cohorts) and diagnosed malignancy 2.7% (1.0-4.6; 7 cohorts). Certainty was very low for ovarian loss and imaging findings and low for recurrence and malignancy. Conclusions: Reported oophorectomy rates in prepubertal-predominant cohorts vary widely and often exceed the low prevalence of diagnosed malignancy, but these data cannot establish how many removals were avoidable. The findings support alignment with existing ovarian-conservation guidance and better reporting of menarchal status, indications for removal and functional follow-up.
