papers.abstract_full: Objectives: We aim to investigate whether preoperative salivary active matrix metalloproteinase-8 (aMMP-8) is associated with the early dental implant-stability trajectory during the first 12 weeks after implant placement. Materials and Methods: This prospective, single-center cohort study included 125 adults receiving one implant each in healed edentulous sites. Unstimulated whole saliva was collected preoperatively for aMMP-8 assessment. Implant stability was assessed by resonance frequency analysis and expressed as mean implant stability quotient (ISQ) at placement (T0) and 4, 8, and 12 weeks. Longitudinal ISQ was analyzed using an unstructured-covariance mixed model for repeated measures with categorical time, adjusted for age, sex, smoking, diabetes status, periodontal status, salivary flow, jaw, implant dimensions, insertion torque, and bone quality. The primary analysis evaluated the global 3-df aMMP-8 × time interaction, followed by Holm-adjusted week-specific contrasts. Results: Of 500 scheduled ISQ measurements, 471 (94.2%) were observed. Six of 125 implants (4.8%) failed during the 12-week follow-up. Mean ISQ decreased from 75.9 ± 8.3 at T0 to 69.8 ± 7.5 at week 4 and subsequently increased to 71.4 ± 6.7 and 73.8 ± 7.6 at weeks 8 and 12, respectively. There was evidence of an aMMP-8 × time interaction (F(3, 112.1) = 8.81; p < 0.001). Each 1-SD higher preoperative ln(aMMP-8), equivalent to approximately a 1.89-fold higher concentration, was not clearly associated with ISQ change from T0 at week 4 (-0.81 ISQ units; 95% CI, -1.85 to 0.23; Holm-adjusted p = 0.126), but was associated with less favorable ISQ change at week 8 (-2.55; 95% CI, -3.75 to -1.35; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001) and week 12 (-3.09; 95% CI, -4.39 to -1.79; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). The adjusted association at T0 was close to null (0.30; 95% CI, -1.07 to 1.66; p = 0.669), and the week-8 and week-12 findings were generally consistent across conventional sensitivity analyses, although the week-12 association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant under some failure-inclusive assumptions. Conclusions: Higher preoperative salivary aMMP-8 was associated with a less favorable early implant-stability trajectory, with differences emerging at 8 weeks and persisting at 12 weeks in the primary analysis. These findings support further evaluation of salivary aMMP-8 as a non-invasive preoperative marker of variability in early implant healing, although the clinical significance of the observed ISQ differences and their implications for implant outcomes remain uncertain.

Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical studies reporting treatment duration, post-treatment follow-up, and recurrent tuberculosis episodes after SCRs for DR-…
papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Short-course regimens (SCRs) are increasingly used to treat drug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB), but data on post-treatment recurrence remain limited. We aimed to estimate the frequency of post-treatment recurrence after SCRs and compare recurrence between SCRs and comparator regimens. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of clinical studies reporting treatment duration, post-treatment follow-up, and recurrent tuberculosis episodes after SCRs for DR-TB. The primary single-arm analysis used a binomial-normal random-effects generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) based on r/A, retaining zero-event cohorts without a continuity correction. Comparative analyses used pooled risk ratios (RRs) and person-time-adjusted incidence rate ratios (IRRs). Results: Twenty-five studies contributed 26 SCR cohorts. In the primary analysis, 98 recurrent tuberculosis episodes occurred among 6954 patients; the pooled proportion was 1.24% (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79-1.93%; 95% prediction interval, 0.24-6.21%). The pooled proportion was 1.20% (95% CI, 0.70-2.03%) for fully oral SCRs, 1.57% (0.85-2.85%) for pretomanid-containing SCRs, 1.55% (0.93-2.56%) for SCRs lasting ≤ 39 weeks, and 1.95% (1.20-3.15%) for SCRs lasting ≤ 36 weeks. In the overall comparative analysis, no statistically significant difference in post-treatment recurrence was observed between SCRs and comparator regimens: the pooled RR was 1.35 (95% CI, 0.34-5.40), and the person-time-adjusted IRR was 1.25 (95% CI, 0.50-3.15). In the randomized controlled trial (RCT) subset, the pooled RR indicated a higher recurrence risk with SCRs (RR, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.25-5.89), whereas the corresponding person-time-adjusted estimate did not show a statistically significant difference (IRR, 1.66; 95% CI, 0.81-3.43). This divergence indicates that comparative estimates are sensitive to how post-treatment follow-up duration is accounted for. Meta-regression identified no statistically significant associations between recurrence frequency and the examined cohort-level clinical characteristics. The certainty of evidence, assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework, was low for the estimated recurrence frequency after fully oral SCRs, very low for the subgroup estimates, and low for the comparative estimates. Conclusions: These findings indicate a low frequency of post-treatment tuberculosis recurrence after SCRs and support the durability of treatment outcomes achieved with these regimens. However, substantial between-study heterogeneity and differences in post-treatment follow-up limit the interpretation of the pooled estimate as a uniform long-term recurrence risk. Further studies with standardized follow-up beginning at treatment completion are needed to provide more precise estimates of long-term outcomes after SCRs.

papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: Long-term treatment options for fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS) remain limited and there is a lack of real-world data on the extended use of nutraceutical formulations containing palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) and acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC). This study describes a cohort treated for 12 months with a fixed multicomponent formulation containing PEA and ALC, followed by an additional visit three months post-treatment. Methods: This retrospective, uncontrolled single-cohort study involved 150 consecutive adults diagnosed with fibromyalgia syndrome (FMS). Participants received a fixed oral formulation comprising palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) 600 mg, acetyl-L-carnitine (ALC) 500 mg, Boswellia serrata 100 mg, vitamin B6 and vitamin E, administered twice daily as an adjunct to stable background therapy. Pain levels were assessed using the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), and the impact of the disease was evaluated with the revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQR) over a period of up to 15 months. Sleep quality was measured using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) for up to 6 months. Missing data were addressed through various methods, including a mixed model, last observation carried forward, delta-adjusted and baseline-carried-forward scenarios, as well as non-responder imputation. Results: Sixty-four patients completed the 12-month course, 45 discontinued (36 for perceived lack of efficacy) and 41 were lost to follow-up. Estimated mean VAS fell from 76.3 to 52.3 at 12 months and FIQR from 73.6 to 56.1; under the worst-case assumption that every non-completer returned to baseline, the mean 12-month change in VAS was -13.0 points (95% CI -15.9 to -10.2). At 6 months, 78.1% of completers reached the FIQR minimal clinically important difference and 59.4% the IMMPACT 30% pain threshold, corresponding to 37.3% and 28.7% of all 150 patients with non-responder imputation; only 20.3% of completers (10.0% of all patients) improved by ≥3 PSQI points. Recorded adverse events occurred in 10.0% of patients. Retention at 12 months was 60.6% (42.7% if patients lost to follow-up were counted as discontinuations). In completers, pain and FIQR three months after the end of treatment were within one point of the 12-month values. Conclusions: In this uncontrolled cohort, 12 months of add-on treatment with a multicomponent formulation containing PEA and ALC was associated with reductions in pain and disease impact, whereas sleep outcomes changed minimally. However, attrition was substantial and partially response-dependent; therefore, the observed changes cannot be attributed to the formulation or its individual components. These descriptive findings support the need for a controlled trial with a duration of at least 12 months.

papers.abstract_full: Although grain size is an important trait in Central Asian (CA) wheat breeding and industry, it remains genetically uncharacterized. We conducted GWAS and QTL mapping using a commercial wheat diversity panel (DP) and segregating population (SP). No genetic or phenotypic variation in grain width (GW) was detected in the studied panel under the conditions examined. For grain length (GL), we identified 37 significant MTAs on chromosomes 1A, 1B, 1D, 2B, 2D, 3A, 3B, 3D, 4B, 5A, 5B, 5D, 6A, 6B, 7A, 7B and 7D. The MTA on chromosome 2D (TaGL2DMTA) was identified by three GWAS models simultaneously. Two loci controlling GL, on chromosomes 2D (TaGL2DQTL) and 3A (TaGL3AQTL), were identified from QTL analysis. Loci on chromosome 2D were detected by complementary GWAS and QTL. TaGL2DMTA, TaGL2DQTL and TaGL3AQTL accounted for 12.4-15.5%, 14.5-18.3%, and 24.4-28.2% of the phenotypic variation, and increased GL by 6.8% (p = 0.0009), 2.3% (p = 0.024) and 4.0% (p = 0.0001), respectively. When these were converted to KASP markers, GL was significantly different between effective and non-effective alleles for TaGL2DMTA (p = 0.001) and TaGL3AQTL (p < 0.003). The validation of TaGL2DQTL highlighted limited effective allele distribution (~3%) in the DP. GL was positively correlated with GWT and TGW in both DP (r = 0.166/p = 0.03 and 0.526/p = 0.001, respectively) and SP (r = 0.212/p = 0.08 and 0.640/p = 0.001, respectively). Despite seasonal variation in GL, heritability was high, with H2 = 0.91 for DP and 0.93 for SP, indicating high genetic stability. Overall, these findings provide new insights into the genetic control of grain size, and highlight the identified loci as promising targets for marker-assisted selection in CA wheat breeding.

papers.abstract_full: Grain protein content (GPC) is an important determinant of rice nutritional and eating quality. In this study, 624 cold-region japonica rice accessions were evaluated for GPC and taste value at Harbin Minzhu, Ulanhot, and a saline-alkali site in the Songnen Plain, and 495 accessions with complete phenotypic and genotypic data were used for genome-wide association analysis. GPC showed significant positive correlations across sites and an entry-mean broad-sense heritability of 0.663. Using 1,527,603 high-quality SNPs, GLM-Q identified 56 significant GPC-associated SNPs, mainly on chromosomes 11 and 7, with site-specific patterns. Annotation of GLM-Q significant SNPs yielded 28 non-redundant positional candidate genes. In GEMMA, chromosome 11 signals did not remain genome-wide significant, whereas chromosome 7 associations remained significant. Haplotypes of Os11g0239500, Os11g0239900, Os07g0264100, and Os03g0244200 differed in GPC and taste value. Joint haplotype analysis of Os11g0239500 and Os07g0264100 classified 319 accessions into four types. Type IV had the lowest mean GPC (7.84%) and the highest mean taste value (81.14), whereas Type I had a mean GPC of 8.78% and a mean taste value of 77.45. The identified candidate genes and haplotypes may be useful for screening cold-region japonica rice with low GPC and high eating quality.

papers.abstract_full: Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is an essential staple crop worldwide, and tillering acts as a key target for molecular breeding because of its critical contribution to grain yield. In this study, a high-tillering dwarf mutant designated htd8 was isolated from an ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS)-mutagenized population of indica rice cultivar 'Shuangkezao (SKZ)'. The mutant exhibits reduced plant height, dramatically increased tiller number, shortened and yellow-chlorotic leaves. Compared with the wild-type (WT), htd8 displays significant decreases in plant height, internode length, panicle branch number and 1000-grain weight, accompanied by a remarkable increase in tiller count. Genetic analysis demonstrated that the htd8 phenotype is governed by a single recessive nuclear gene. By bulked segregant analysis (BSA) sequencing combined with fine mapping, the candidate gene was delimited to a 0.81 Mb genomic interval on rice chromosome 11, where two known tillering-related genes D27 and ZEBRA2 were excluded. Exogenous hormone assays revealed that htd8 had decreased sensitivity to exogenous GA3 but enhanced sensitivity to the strigolactone analog GR24, and both GA3 and GR24 could repress tiller outgrowth in the mutant. Under salt stress and PEG-simulated osmotic stress, htd8 achieved a notably higher survival rate relative to WT. The mutant accumulated more proline (Pro), maintained lower malondialdehyde (MDA) levels, and showed elevated leaf abscisic acid (ABA) content together with the upregulated expression of ABA biosynthetic-related genes. Transcriptome profiling of tiller buds indicated that HTD8 modulates rice tillering and plant architecture by coordinating brassinosteroid, auxin, gibberellin and strigolactone signaling pathways, as well as carbon metabolism redistribution. This work provides theoretical insights into the molecular mechanism underlying high-tillering dwarfism and supplies valuable genetic resources for high-yield and stress-tolerant rice molecular breeding.

papers.abstract_full: Soybean seed protein content is a polygenic quantitative trait, and dissecting its genetic architecture is critical for advancing high-protein soybean molecular breeding. In this study, an F5 recombinant inbred line (RIL) population with 174 lines derived from a cross between high-protein cultivar Kedou 48 and low-protein cultivar Kedou 61 was phenotyped for seed protein content across four distinct growing environments. Genotyping was performed using 25,663 high-quality single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), followed by multi-locus genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Phenotypic data revealed seed protein content ranged from 31.24% to 46.65% across the population, with a broad-sense heritability of 0.89. In total, 54 quantitative trait nucleotides (QTNs) linked to seed protein content were detected via 11 multi-locus GWAS algorithms; among these, 16 QTNs were classified as stable QTNs because they were detected by at least two GWAS models within the same environment and/or in at least two environments, and 33 QTNs overlapped with previously published seed protein quantitative trait loci (QTLs). Integrating linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay estimation, seed tissue expression profiles, parental resequencing-derived non-synonymous variants, and germplasm haplotype characterization, three candidate genes were prioritized: Glyma.08G246400 (AFP3/NINJA-like transcriptional repressor), Glyma.09G154600 (LRR receptor-like protein kinase), and Glyma.19G224000 (translation initiation factor IF-2). Haplotype analyses using eligible accessions from the collaborative 2898-accession soybean resequencing panel identified significant haplotype-protein associations for all three genes after adjustment for germplasm type, with divergent haplotype distributions among Soja, landraces, and improved cultivars. This work provides stable QTNs supported by repeated detection, three biologically plausible candidate genes, and protein-associated haplotypes for further mechanistic and breeding evaluation in high-protein early-maturing soybean.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Self-reported hearing impairment and edentulism are common age-related conditions, yet whether they act as independent markers of accumulating chronic disease multimorbidity remains uncertain. This study characterized their population trajectories and examined their associations with multimorbidity, testing cross-national reproducibility. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Using four waves (2011-2018) of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS) with external validation in the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS), we characterized self-reported hearing impairment and edentulism trajectories with latent class linear mixed models among 17,585 participants and, in 15,842 Wave 1 participants, examined associations with chronic disease multimorbidity after extensive covariate adjustment. RESULTS: Self-reported hearing impairment prevalence rose from 54.6% to 66.4% across waves; edentulism ranged from 4.5% to 8.4%. A single-class model best fitted both outcomes, with significant per-wave increases in self-reported hearing impairment (0.051 per wave). Self-reported hearing impairment was associated with higher odds of two or more (OR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.31-1.53) and three or more (OR = 1.43, 95% CI 1.28-1.60) chronic conditions, replicated in Wave 4 (OR = 1.40 and 1.50) and in HRS (OR = 1.38). In a prospective analysis of participants free of multimorbidity at baseline, self-reported hearing impairment predicted incident multimorbidity at Wave 4 (OR = 1.35 in the age- and sex-adjusted model; OR = 1.28 in the fully adjusted model). By contrast, edentulism showed no consistent independent association with multimorbidity; its crude association was explained by age. CONCLUSIONS: A single self-reported hearing question is a sensitive, dose-dependent, and cross-nationally reproducible indicator of coexisting multiple diseases in middle-aged and older adults and merits consideration as a low-cost first-line indicator in primary care. Edentulism was not independently associated with multimorbidity after accounting for age.

papers.abstract_full: Background: Menopause is accompanied by substantial interindividual variation in hormonal, metabolic, cardiovascular, skeletal, and thrombotic phenotypes. Although the genetics of reproductive ageing and individual menopause-associated traits are increasingly characterised, the cross-phenotype architecture of individual menopause-relevant germline variants remains less well defined. Methods: We performed a variant-centred genomic analysis of 31 prespecified menopause-relevant germline variants. Cross-trait evidence comprised 766 variant-trait records across 52 phenotypes and was integrated with a targeted Pan-UK Biobank phenome-wide association study (PheWAS; 1462 tests across 57 endpoints), clinically relevant outcome analyses, linkage disequilibrium assessment, FinnGen R12 venous thromboembolism (VTE) associations, regional fine-mapping, and molecular annotation. Association strength, between-study heterogeneity, phenotypic breadth and sharing, and locus resolution were evaluated as distinct evidence dimensions. Results: In total, 25 of 31 variants showed at least one cross-trait association at p < 1 × 10-5 and 21 reached genome-wide significance. Phenotypic breadth varied markedly, from restricted profiles to 16 associated phenotypes, and strong associations frequently coexisted with substantial between-study heterogeneity. In Pan-UK Biobank, 222 associations involving 25 variants met false-discovery-rate correction, spanning hormonal, reproductive, cardiometabolic, skeletal, nutritional, hepatic, and neurological phenotypes. Cross-phenotype reconstruction identified recurrent connectivity through sex hormone-binding globulin, testosterone, adiposity, lipid, and skeletal traits, while linkage disequilibrium analyses distinguished phenotypic sharing from genetic redundancy. Clinically, F5 rs6025 and F2 rs1799963 showed strong VTE associations in FinnGen (OR 2.387 and 1.921, respectively), but markedly different locus resolution: rs6025 had posterior inclusion probability (PIP) 0.979 and constituted a single-variant 95% credible set, whereas rs1799963 had PIP 0.596 within a four-variant credible set. Conclusions: Menopause-relevant germline variation exhibits heterogeneous cross-phenotype architectures in which association strength, phenotypic breadth, between-study consistency, genetic independence, and locus resolution are not interchangeable. This variant-centred framework provides a basis for evaluating inherited susceptibility relevant to menopause and hormone exposure, while prospective individual-level studies remain necessary before translation into risk prediction or treatment selection.

papers.abstract_full: Background/Objectives: To evaluate, in an exploratory pilot study, the influence of slice thickness and monoenergetic (ME) level on quantitative and qualitative image quality of ultra-high-resolution (UHR) photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) in rectal cancer (RC). Methods: This prospective pilot study enrolled 21 patients with suspected RC undergoing pre-treatment PCD-CT between July 2023 and February 2025. All underwent a QuantumPlus portal venous phase, whose 3 mm/60 keV reconstruction served as the standard reference, plus a separate pelvic UHR acquisition. Sixteen UHR reconstructions were generated (0.6-3 mm; 45-70 keV). Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) and noise were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. Three readers independently rated overall image quality, perceived noise, mesorectal fascia (MRF) sharpness and lesion conspicuity relative to the reference; ratings were analyzed using mixed model ordinal regression. The primary analysis was the within-UHR comparison of reconstruction settings; the comparison with the reference, which differed in contrast phase and acquisition parameters, was descriptive. Results: Nineteen patients (mean age 61.7 ± 10.7 years, 73.7% male) were included. CNR showed a significant slice thickness-ME level interaction (p < 0.001), ranging from 4.85 ± 2.43 (3 mm/45 keV) to 0.86 ± 1.04 (0.6 mm/70 keV). SNR increased and noise decreased with thicker slices, while both decreased with higher ME levels (all p < 0.001). ME level influenced all four qualitative parameters (all p < 0.001); slice thickness significantly affected overall quality and perceived noise (p < 0.001) but not MRF sharpness or lesion conspicuity (p ≥ 0.115). Overall quality was rated favorably in 82.9% at 70 keV versus 45.6% at 45 keV. Lesion conspicuity reached 71.9-86.0% favorable ratings, whereas perceived noise was consistently rated worse than the reference, and UHR SNR remained below the reference in all settings. In a descriptive pooled summary, 3 mm/60 keV (68.0%) and 2 mm/70 keV (66.2%) were rated favorably most often, with overlapping confidence intervals. Conclusions: Slice thickness and ME level markedly influence UHR PCD-CT image quality in RC. One candidate working reconstruction for future validation is 3 mm at 60 keV, with 2 mm at 70 keV as a plausible alternative. Because the reference differed in acquisition and contrast phase and no diagnostic endpoint was assessed, these results do not establish a diagnostic benefit of UHR PCD-CT.

papers.abstract_full: Artificial insemination is used widely in the swine industry, resulting in increasing focus on the traits of boar semen and methods for their genetic improvement. This study analyzed 21,160 phenotypic records of fresh semen derived from 492 Large White boars and 231 Landrace boars. The semen traits included the semen volume (VOL), sperm concentration (CON), sperm motility (MOT), and abnormal sperm rate (ABN). Single-trait and multi-trait repeatability models were used to assess the overall genetic parameters of semen traits, while random regression models were applied to examine trends in heritability changes over the collection period. In addition, multi-trait repeatability models were also used to estimate genetic and phenotypic correlations among the traits. The single-trait repeatability model indicated heritability estimates of VOL, MOT, CON, and ABN of 0.23, 0.09, 0.22, and 0.07, respectively, for Large White boars, with corresponding values for Landrace boars of 0.42, 0.06, 0.16, and 0.17. The respective values calculated by the multi-trait repeatability model were 0.23, 0.08, 0.22 and 0.09 for Large White boars and 0.43, 0.06, 0.20 and 0.17 for Landrace boars. Sperm motility, sperm concentration, and abnormal sperm rate showed low-to-moderate heritability. Semen volume showed moderate heritability in Large White boars and high heritability in Landrace boars. The random regression results indicated heritability estimates for VOL, MOT, CON, and ABN of 0.24-0.53, 0.05-0.08, 0.13-0.23, and 0.03-0.31, respectively, for Large White boars and 0.08-0.31, 0.02-0.15, 0.26-0.53, and 0.12-0.17 for Landrace boars. Significant negative genetic correlations were found between VOL and CON in both breeds (-0.54 for Large White and -0.73 for Landrace), and between VOL and MOT in Landrace. These findings will facilitate more precise selection to improve boar semen quality and reproductive efficiency in the swine industry.

papers.abstract_full: Background: Hepatic arterial infusion (HAI) chemotherapy for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) is delivered through a port-catheter system implanted percutaneously by interventional radiology or surgically. Previous studies have pooled device complications across access methods as event counts, but have not synthesised the technical performance and durability of fully percutaneous insertion at the patient level. Methods: Medline, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for studies published from 2000 onward reporting adults with CRLM undergoing HAI port insertion. Primary analyses were restricted to fully percutaneous implanted ports, using outcome-specific, patient-level numerators and denominators; a study using surgical arterial cutdown was added in sensitivity analyses. Risk of bias in the device outcomes was assessed at item level for patient selection, completeness of data, outcome ascertainment and selective reporting, with Cochrane RoB 2 used additionally for the single randomised trial. Random-effects proportion meta-analyses used the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation and the DerSimonian-Laird estimator, with a binomial generalised linear mixed model (GLMM) as an alternative. Outcomes with inconsistent definitions or denominators were synthesised narratively. Results: Fifteen studies contributed 811 patients, 654 of whom underwent percutaneous insertion. One study was randomised, five prospective and nine retrospective; three reported a surgical comparator arm. Risk of bias in the device outcomes was low in one study, moderate in six and high in eight. Eleven studies (423 patients) of fully percutaneous implanted ports contributed to the primary analyses. Technical success was reported explicitly by eight and achieved in 276 of 278 patients (99.3%, exact 95% CI 97.4-99.9%); with only two failures, pooled models added little. Device-attributable definitive failure, meaning permanent discontinuation of HAI because of the device, occurred in 39 of 374 patients (crude 10.4%) over observation periods that varied widely; the random-effects estimate was 6.9% (95% CI 2.1-13.7%; I2 = 74.5%; GLMM 6.9%, 3.0-15.2%), and 11.6% (95% CI 6.3-18.0%) in the six studies at low or moderate risk of bias. Catheter dislodgement affected a pooled 5.8% (95% CI 1.6-11.6%), and 14.8% where the port was checked angiographically before every course or every four weeks; hepatic arterial occlusion affected 3.4% (95% CI 0.9-7.0%; four studies). Revision was required in 56% and 59% of percutaneous patients in the two series reporting it. Conclusions: Percutaneous insertion of HAI ports rarely failed technically in these series, but reintervention was common and permanent loss of HAI to a device problem within the follow-up reported was estimated at 6.9% in the primary analysis and 11.6% in studies at lower risk of bias, with more problems detected where the device was monitored more closely. Catheter-tip technique, follow-up duration and intensity of device surveillance are possible, unproven contributors to heterogeneity. These predominantly observational data support the feasibility of percutaneous access, not patient suitability for HAI chemotherapy.

One study was randomised, five prospective and nine retrospective; three reported a surgical comparator arm.
Risk of bias in the device outcomes was low in one study, moderate in six and high in eight.

papers.abstract_full: Bone strain and remodeling are important factors affecting bone strength. Better characterizing the relationship between these factors in response to acute loading will improve our understanding of bone metabolism in relation to daily physical activities. The purpose of this study was to evaluate colocalization between finite element-estimated bone strain and [18F]sodium fluoride ([18F]NaF) positron emission tomography (PET) imaging-estimated bone remodeling in the tibial diaphysis in response to acute exercise. We hypothesized that the exercise-induced change in standardized uptake values would be greatest in regions of higher strain. 26 participants underwent bilateral PET-magnetic resonance imaging (PET-MRI) scans before and after a bout of stair ascent and descent exercise. Finite element analysis was performed to calculate principal strain distributions in the tibial diaphysis. [18F]NaF standardized uptake values (SUV) were calculated from pre- and post-exercise PET data and mapped to the tibial surface. Mean pre-exercise and exercise-induced change in SUV were calculated and compared between regions defined by strain percentile. Both normalized mean pre-exercise and exercise-induced change in [18F]NaF SUV increased with maximum principal strain in a pattern suggesting an exponential relationship. Pre-exercise and exercise-induced change in SUV were notably much greater in the region of highest maximum principal strains (estimated marginal means = 76.9 and 71.0 percentile, respectively) when compared to all other regions of the tibial diaphysis (≤ 61.1 and ≤ 57.0 percentile, respectively, p < 0.001). This study is the first to directly show a relationship between bone mechanical loads and acute [18F]NaF uptake in humans in vivo. Our results highlight the influence of tensile strain magnitude on bone metabolic activity in response to acute loading. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of a combined finite element analysis and [18F] PET approach to interrogate relationships between bone loading and bone metabolic response to acute exercise. This study aimed to understand the relationship between bone loading and bone metabolic activity, important factors influencing bone health. Before and after exercise, 26 participants underwent imaging following injection with [18F]sodium fluoride, a radiotracer that localizes to areas in bone with increased perfusion and/or increased remodeling activity. Tracer uptake was spatially compared to bone loading distribution, calculated using personalized models. Exercise-induced change in tracer uptake was increased in regions of high tensile strain, highlighting the importance of loading magnitude in bone metabolism. This combined imaging and modeling approach is a promising method to interrogate relationships between loading and bone metabolism.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Elevated concentrations of lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)] are a well-established risk factor for the development of coronary artery diseases and acute myocardial infarction (AMI). The objective of the present study was to analyze the association between plasma concentrations of Lp(a) and long-term all-cause mortality among individuals with a history of hospitalized AMI. METHODS: The analysis was based on data from 617 patients with a history of AMI recruited by the Augsburg Myocardial Infarction Registry and examined in a follow-up visit within the scope of the KORA Family Heart Study in 1996 and 1997 (median time between AMI and follow-up examination: 6.2 years). In addition, 545 siblings of the patients were included in the study and underwent examination. The examination included venous blood sampling and a patient interview. Plasma concentrations of Lp(a) were measured using a latex-enhanced immunoassay. Information on vital status was obtained in November 2025 in a comprehensive mortality follow-up [median follow-up time: 18.2 years (IQR: 10.8-27.7)]. Follow-up time was calculated from examination date to date of death or censoring. Kaplan-Meier curves were used to display estimated survival probability of Lp(a) high (≥ 50 mg/dL) and low (< 50 mg/dL) group. Multivariable adjusted Cox regression models with restricted cubic splines were used to analyze the association between Lp(a) concentrations and long-term all-cause mortality after AMI. RESULTS: Kaplan-Meier curves and log rank test (p value: 0.273) demonstrated no differences in long-term all-cause mortality between the high and low Lp(a) group. The multivariable adjusted Cox regression confirmed the absence of a significant association between Lp(a) concentrations and total mortality (HR for the high Lp(a) group: 1.04, 95%CI: 0.84-1.28, p value: 0.734). Several sensitivity analyses, including a mixed model on a sample including siblings of the AMI patients (HR for the high Lp(a) group: 1.09) and a more thoroughly adjusted model including additional potential confounders confirmed the results of the main model. CONCLUSIONS: In this study, no association between elevated Lp(a) and long-term mortality was detected. Due to the observational character of the study, no conclusions about treatment of patients with elevated Lp(a) can be made and results must be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis generating.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Inflammatory stimuli are associated with onset of anorexia nervosa (AN) but whether inflammation occurs in the brain of AN is unknown. The primary objective is to determine whether [18F]FEPPA total distribution volume ([18F]FEPPA VT), PET index of translocator protein density and inflammatory marker of gliosis, is elevated in AN in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), ventral striatum (VS), dorsal caudate (DC), dorsal putamen (DP), thalamus, orbitofrontal cortex and insula. Secondary objectives are to determine the relationship of [18F]FEPPA VT in ACC to rumination severity and [18F]FEPPA VT to body mass index (BMI). METHODS: [18F]FEPPA VT was measured in 20 medication free AN participants and 20 healthy controls. Correlations of [18F]FEPPA VT with rumination severity, and BMI, were determined. RESULTS: [18F]FEPPA VT was elevated in AN in all ROI (linear mixed model (LMM), group effect, P = 4×10-7), particularly ACC, VS, DC and thalamus (mean 52% elevation; LMM, region by group interaction, P = 4×10-4). ACC [18F]FEPPA VT correlated positively with eating concerns (Eating Disorder Examination, r = 0.58, P = .007; Inventory of Depression and Anxiety Symptoms-II, r = 0.66, P = .002). There were no significant correlations between [18F]FEPPA VT and BMI. CONCLUSIONS: Greater [18F]FEPPA VT is strong evidence for neuroinflammation and gliosis, particularly in ACC, VS, DC and thalamus in AN. Given such, it may be of interest to assess interventions that influence gliosis towards curative roles in future clinical trials in AN.

papers.abstract_full: Single-trait and multi-trait genome-wide association studies (C-GWAS) were performed on 18 carcass- and growth-related traits in a Pekin duck × Liancheng White duck F₂ population (n = 242; slaughtered at 70 d) using 12.8 million SNPs. Single-trait GWAS identified major-effect loci for carcass weight and half-eviscerated weight on chromosome 2 (104.68 Mb), for leg muscle weight on chromosome 2 (57.91 Mb), and for abdominal fat weight and skin fat thickness on chromosome 3 (88.46 Mb), revealing heterogeneous genetic architectures ranging from major-effect variants to polygenic backgrounds; the broad signal intervals were consistent with long-range LD in the F₂ population. Multi-trait C-GWAS substantially improved detection power, identifying 79022 genome-wide significant SNPs (P < 5×10⁻⁸), of which 69.9% were located within gene regions-markedly higher than the genomic background (∼45%). Functional enrichment of the 7,889 annotated candidate genes highlighted cell adhesion, actin cytoskeleton organization, and focal adhesion as core biological themes, with the IgSF-CAM signaling pathway (apla04517, Padjust = 2.9×10⁻¹²) as the most significantly enriched KEGG pathway-a signal not detected in single-trait analyses. Tissue-specific eQTL colocalization identified liver (33471 pairs) and muscle (29426 pairs) as the primary effector tissues, with MLH3 showing pleiotropic signals across multiple tissues, NGEF exhibiting muscle-specific enrichment, and PINK1 dominant in liver. Integrating SNP annotation, functional enrichment, and eQTL colocalization, six high-confidence candidate genes (MLH3, NGEF, PINK1, PRDM16, PTK2, and CADM2) were prioritized. Among these, NGEF (implicated in myocyte fusion) and PRDM16 (involved in adipocyte differentiation) represent promising targets for future functional validation and marker-assisted breeding. These findings demonstrate the utility of C-GWAS for dissecting pleiotropic genetic architectures in poultry and provide a prioritized resource for genetic improvement of duck carcass traits.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Depression is a leading contributor to morbidity and disability in children and adolescents. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a guideline-recommended first-line treatment, but access is constrained by therapist supply, distance, and stigma. Internet-based CBT is a scalable adjunct in adults, yet regulatory-grade evidence in Chinese pediatric samples remains limited. OBJECTIVE: This trial will determine whether a smartphone-delivered CBT-based digital therapeutic is superior to a matched health-education placebo in reducing depressive symptoms in Chinese children and adolescents with major depressive disorder (MDD), and characterize its safety. METHODS: This is a prospective, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled superiority trial at 4 tertiary-A hospitals in mainland China. Children and adolescents aged 8-17 years meeting DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [Fifth Edition]) criteria for current MDD without psychotic features and scoring above 30 on the Children's Depression Rating Scale-Revised (CDRS-R) at screening will be randomized 1:1 to the investigational digital therapeutic (Model WL-PD) or a visually matched health-education placebo. Both arms receive 8 weeks of structured content on an identical schedule; participants with CDRS-R ≥57 additionally receive open-label fluoxetine under weight-banded dosing. The primary end point is CDRS-R total-score reduction from baseline to week 8. Secondary end points include CDRS-R change at weeks 1 to 6; response and remission rates; Clinical Global Impression scores; the Children's Depression Inventory; the Conners' Parent Symptom Questionnaire; and a week-8 device-performance evaluation. Safety end points include adverse-event, serious adverse-event, and device-defect incidence. The planned sample of 214 participants (107 per arm) is powered at 80% to detect a between-arm difference of 4.6 CDRS-R points (assumed control SD 10.7) with a 1-sided α of .025 and 20% inflation for attrition. The primary analysis is an analysis of covariance on the full analysis set adjusting for baseline CDRS-R, severity category, fluoxetine exposure, and site; superiority is declared if the lower bound of the 2-sided 95% CI excludes zero, with a mixed model for repeated measures as a sensitivity analysis. RESULTS: The trial opened to enrollment in March 2026; recruitment is ongoing, with a planned close in December 2026. The last week-8 visit is expected in the first quarter of 2027, and the primary analysis the following year. CONCLUSIONS: The trial addresses 3 recognized gaps in the pediatric digital therapeutics literature: a rigorous, structurally matched blinded control condition, recruitment beyond a single site, and integration of guideline-concordant pharmacotherapy. Because recruitment is confined to tertiary hospitals and excludes participants with prominent suicidality or comorbidity, findings will apply to supervised use in specialist services rather than unselected community care. papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Potential dental health benefits, including pH buffering, have been demonstrated for nitrate in placebo-controlled studies when consumed one or several hours before sugar intake. However, its immediate local effect when co-administered with sugar is unclear. Our aim was to test the local effect of adding nitrate to a sugar rinse on human saliva acidification. METHODS: A double-blind, crossover study was conducted with three periods. In each period, 18 adults, equally distributed between men and women (n = 9 each), aged 25.4 ± 3.8 (mean ± SD), with normal salivary flow, rinsed for 2 min using 10 mL of one of the following rinses: spinach-only (blended spinach providing 8 mm nitrate), spinach+sucrose (blended spinach providing 8 mm nitrate + 20% sucrose), or sucrose-only (20% sucrose). Unstimulated saliva was collected at baseline and every 3 min up to 24 min. pH, lactate, nitrate, and nitrite were measured using Reflectoquant®. The effect of treatment and time was assessed using a linear mixed model (α = 0.05). Nitrate reduction capacity was determined in vitro using baseline saliva. RESULTS: All saliva samples demonstrated nitrate reduction activity. The lowest pH values were observed 6 min after rinsing, with all groups differing from each other: sucrose only (6.56 ± 0.38; mean ± SD), spinach+sucrose (6.83 ± 0.37), spinach only (7.15 ± 0.44, no pH drop). The pH returned to baseline values 12 min after the spinach+sucrose rinse, but not after the sucrose-only rinse at any time point. Nitrate and nitrite concentrations increased in saliva after using spinach-containing rinses, returning to their baseline levels after 6 min and 12 min. Lower lactate levels were detected after 12 min, suggesting proton consumption during nitrate metabolism in the spinach+sucrose group. CONCLUSION: Adding a low dose of nitrate to a sucrose rinse limited sugar-induced salivary acidification in vivo, supporting the potential for topical nitrate strategies to reduce sugar acidogenicity. This study explored whether mixing a small amount of nitrate from spinach with sugar (i.e., 5 mg nitrate per 2 g sucrose) could reduce the drop in pH that usually occurs in saliva after consuming sugar. When sugar is eaten, bacteria in the mouth produce acid, which can lead to tooth demineralization over time. Nitrate is a natural compound found in vegetables like spinach and can be converted by bacteria in the mouth into other substances that may help reduce saliva acidogenicity. In this study, 18 healthy adults participated in three separate test sessions. In each session, they rinsed their mouths with one of three solutions: sugar-only, spinach-only, or spinach plus sugar. Saliva samples were collected before and after each rinse (up to 24 min) to measure pH (acidity), nitrate, nitrite, and lactate levels. The results showed that rinsing with the sugar-only solution caused a drop in salivary pH. However, in the spinach plus sugar condition, the drop in pH was less severe and recovered more quickly. This suggests that nitrate may help reduce the acid effects of sugar in the mouth. Saliva from all participants was also able to convert nitrate to nitrite, which supports this effect. These findings support the idea that natural nitrate, when delivered together with sugar, could help mitigate pH drops. However, more studies are needed to test whether this approach can help prevent dental demineralization in real-life settings.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Apolipoprotein 1 (APOL1) risk alleles (G1 and G2) are major genetic drivers of APOL1-associated kidney disease in populations of African ancestry. Prior studies implicated membrane-associated channel activity and ion dysregulation in APOL1 cytotoxicity, but how APOL1 risk alleles engage intracellular membranes, disrupt endoplasmic reticulum calcium, and are handled by quality-control pathways remains incompletely defined. METHODS: We used a split-green fluorescent protein topology system to visualize and quantify APOL1 membrane insertion and domain-deletion mutants to define structural requirements for insertion and toxicity. Endoplasmic reticulum calcium was monitored using a genetically encoded fluorescent, endoplasmic reticulum-specific calcium indicator. APOL1 degradation was assessed using autophagy and proteasome modulators, immunoblotting, and LC3 colocalization. In vivo relevance was tested in transgenic Drosophila nephrocytes expressing human APOL1 alleles with or without dietary rapamycin. Rapamycin reduced APOL1 protein levels, improved cell viability, and mitigated risk allele-induced nephrocyte hypertrophy and filtration dysfunction in vivo. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identified enhanced endoplasmic reticulum membrane insertion, endoplasmic reticulum calcium depletion, and autophagy-lysosomal clearance as linked features of APOL1 risk allele toxicity.

papers.abstract_full: The causal effect between major depressive disorder (MDD) and asthma phenotypes was rarely evaluated. The objective of our study was to not only assess the potential causal links of MDD on asthma phenotypes, but also the mediating effect of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) on asthma phenotypes caused by MDD. By using 2-sample Mendelian randomization (MR), Bayesian weighted MR, and mediation analysis, we explored the potential causal effect of MDD and the mediating effect of FEV1 on asthma phenotypes (childhood asthma, adult asthma, obesity asthma, allergic asthma, and nonallergic asthma) from the genome-wide association studies database. Furthermore, genetic correlation was also evaluated by the analysis of linkage disequilibrium score regression. We additionally performed multivariable MR (MVMR) analyses including body mass index and smoking to evaluate MDD estimates for asthma phenotypes. The results of univariable MR and MVMR analyses supported associations of MDD with adult asthma, obesity asthma, and allergic asthma, and MVMR analysis indicated the potential association of MDD with child asthma and nonallergic asthma. FEV1 indicated a mediated effect of MDD on adult asthma, obesity asthma, allergic asthma, and nonallergic asthma. Our analyses supported associations of MDD with asthma phenotypes. The mediation analysis suggested that FEV1 may mediate part of these associations of MDD on adult asthma, obesity asthma, allergic asthma, and nonallergic asthma.

papers.abstract: The rapidly changing cultural contexts over the past century modified the genetic factors that influence smoking initiation (SI). Using data from nearly seven million respondents, we conducted genome-wide associations study (GWAS) meta-analyses stratified by sex and generation across European, East Asian, African American, and Latino genetic ancestry populations. papers.abstract_full: The rapidly changing cultural contexts over the past century modified the genetic factors that influence smoking initiation (SI). Using data from nearly seven million respondents, we conducted genome-wide associations study (GWAS) meta-analyses stratified by sex and generation across European, East Asian, African American, and Latino genetic ancestry populations. Sex and generation, but not genetic ancestry, moderate both the SNP-based heritability estimates and associations with individual loci. Specifically, SI is more heritable in females and younger generations. Furthermore, the impact of both discrete policy changes that target smoking and the gradual cultural redefinition of smoking norms across sex and generation are captured within the patterns of cross-trait genetic correlations between SI and extant smoking-relevant phenotypes. Robust cross-ancestry genetic correlations allowed us to meta-analyze the results across subsamples, identifying 1,717 loci associated with SI, including both main and moderated associations for either moderator. Genome-wide heterogeneity analyses identified 45 sex-specific loci and 7 generation-specific loci with distinct associations with SI. Finemapping analyses highlighted 389 and 304 loci with distinct patterns of potential causal variants by sex and generation. Accordingly, sex- and generation-specific macrosocial contexts dynamically influence the genetic architecture of SI, underscoring the need to consider gene-environment interplay for health behaviors as societal norms evolve.

papers.abstract: Genetic effects on common disease are mediated through many genes in multiple cell types, yet how networks connect genome-wide genetic risk to core disease genes remains unclear. One key limitation is that disease-related gene networks are likely cell type-specific, but these are poorly captured by bulk and pseudobulk coexpression networks. papers.abstract_full: Genetic effects on common disease are mediated through many genes in multiple cell types, yet how networks connect genome-wide genetic risk to core disease genes remains unclear. One key limitation is that disease-related gene networks are likely cell type-specific, but these are poorly captured by bulk and pseudobulk coexpression networks. Here we used population-scale single-cell immune transcriptomes to decompose interindividual gene coexpression into cell type-shared and -specific networks, which have nearly opposite properties. Shared network hubs were enriched in constrained housekeeping genes, whereas cell type-specific hubs were dynamically expressed, rapidly evolving, and enriched in cell type-matched enhancers and transcription factors. Specific hubs enriched for immune disease GWAS heritability, Mendelian genes, and drug targets; these enrichments were absent or weak for non-immune disease and shared hubs. Gene-gene network edges enriched for causal trans regulation identified by trans eQTLs and perturb-seq, with shared hubs skewed to upstream regulators and specific hubs skewed to downstream disease-proximal genes. Specific hubs increased the relative success of genetically supported immune drug targets from 1.7-fold to 2.7-fold; for example, the lupus drug target BAFF is a monocyte hub connected to the Mendelian gene TREX1 and interferon-responsive genes. Overall, accounting for shared housekeeping networks reveals that cell type-specific networks funnel genetic risk into downstream and dynamic core disease genes.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear.  Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation.  Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.

papers.abstract: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals. Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer. papers.abstract_full: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals. Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer. However, the influence of Neanderthal variants on germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated. Here, we evaluated genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits for 17 cancer types for Neanderthal ancestry. Twelve cancers have multiple Neanderthal alleles significantly associated with variation in risk. Next, we fine-mapped these risk loci and identified 32 associations across seven cancers where Neanderthal variants are likely causal (>= posterior inclusion probability). Fine-mapped loci include Neanderthal alleles that both increase and decrease cancer risk. Nine of the 32 Neanderthal associations, including the high frequency BNC2 Neanderthal variants, have signatures of adaptive introgression, and several suggest evidence of both mediated and antagonistic pleiotropy. Finally, we tested for enrichment of cancer heritability in genomic regions with Neanderthal ancestry. As expected, Neanderthal variants are depleted of heritability for most cancers. However, Neanderthal variants were enriched for heritability in breast cancer GWAS in both East Asian and Europeans, and this enrichment replicated using individual-level UK Biobank data. These results suggest that Neanderthal alleles that influence germline cancer risk were largely selected against. However, introgressed Neanderthal variants implicated in many cancers persist, potentially due to adaptive pleiotropic effects. This evolutionary perspective provides new insights into the complex evolution and etiology of cancer risk among modern human populations.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Background  The unique environment of Burkina Faso, characterized by diverse agroecological zones and variable climatic conditions, presents a challenging yet informative context to understand the genetic adaptations of native taurine cattle populations. Local livestock populations provide important means of livelihoods and have significant economic and cultural values. This study aimed to investigate the genomic signatures of adaptation to different environments in local Lobi and Gourounsi cattle populations. Methods  We employed a landscape genomics approach on a dataset of 342 animals sampled from different environmental zones in Burkina Faso. Climate data including temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, wind speed and water vapor pressure were retrieved for the sampling locations. We assessed genotype-environment associations using a latent factor mixed model and identified significant associations after correcting for multiple testing. Results  The analysis revealed 41 SNPs significantly associated with at least one climatic variable. These SNPs overlapped 141 protein-coding genes involved in reproduction, environmental adaptation and energy trade-offs. These genes are involved in processes such as glucose/lipid metabolism, resource allocation, taste and olfactory perception and response to infectious diseases. The results also highlighted potential adaptations to hot and cold temperatures and suggest a possible adjustment to long-distance walking. Conclusions  These findings provide insights into the genomic adaptations of taurine cattle populations in Burkina Faso to their local environment. The identified genes and biological processes contribute to understanding the mechanisms behind adaptation to climate, energy balance and disease resistance. Our results have implications for livestock management and breeding strategies, as they shed light on the genetic basis of traits related to productivity, resilience and adaptation. Further research and validation might help to fully comprehend the functional significance of these genetic associations and their potential applications in breeding programs and conservation efforts. Overall, this study contributes to the broader field of landscape genomics and enhances our understanding of the genetic adaptations of taurine cattle in the face of environmental challenges.

papers.abstract_full: The interplay between promyelocytic leukemia nuclear bodies (PML NBs) and viral infections is complex and multifaceted, with viruses often engaging in a delicate balance of exploitation and evasion of host immune responses. It is well-established that incoming human papillomavirus (HPV) virions associate with PML NBs; however, the mechanism by which HPV targets PML NBs to facilitate early transcription and replication remains elusive. We have shown that HPV genomes are delivered to the nucleus inside membrane-bound vesicles during mitosis and that PML proteins are recruited to HPV-harboring nuclear vesicles prior to egress. Herein, we demonstrate that the PML isoform II (PMLII), but not other PML isoforms, is selectively attracted to incoming HPV still residing in transport vesicles. Using individual PML NB isoform and HPV16 minor protein, L2, over-expression experiments in HeLa cells, we conclude that PML II binds to the lipids of the HPV harbouring membrane-bound vesicles rather than L2. This is in line with previous observations that PML II is the only isoform binding to lipid droplets in the nucleus. We observed that the association of PML NBs with the HPV16 viral genome was transient and lost over time. We also found that nuclear Phospholipase C β4 and γ1 colocalize with PML II-L1 complexes in infected cells. Our data support a model in which PML II contributes to the establishment of early HPV16 infection by organizing host lipid regulatory factors at incoming viral transport vesicles. Author summary  Promyelocytic leukemia nuclear bodies (PML NBs) are dynamic subnuclear structures involved in antiviral defense, DNA repair, transcriptional regulation and tumor suppression. Despite their antiviral role, HPV exploits PML NBs after nuclear entry, associating its genome with PML proteins, promoting early transcription and infection by shielding the genome from immune responses and degradation. Here, we provide evidence that PML isoform II is preferentially recruited to incoming viral transport vesicles through its interaction with lipids rather than the L2 protein. The association of certain Phospholipases C with the PML II–L1 complex suggests that PML II interacts with lipid-containing HPV16 transport vesicles and may facilitate their PLC- mediated resolution.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Exchanging three-dimensional plant reconstructions between measurement and modeling workflows presents significant challenges. PhenoFrame is introduced as a shared descriptor and software suite that offers both a skeleton mode, utilizing observed leaf centerlines, and a procedural mode, in which each centerline is replaced by fitted parameters. A total of 324 sorghum plants and 3,317 repeated scans of 80 maize plants were converted into both modes. For sorghum, the median descriptor size was reduced from 9.6 to 4.5 kB per plant, with a median mode-to-mode Chamfer distance of 0.65 cm (0.46 cm for maize). For 9 of 13 sorghum traits, procedural-mode estimates reached a broad-sense heritability of at least 0.20 (10 of 13 for voxel-derived traits), as did all 13 maize traits. A descriptor-based stochastic generator approximated the marginal trait distributions, overstating the mean absolute between-node leaf-angle correlation (0.74 versus 0.25 in actual plants). Genome-wide association analysis of the descriptor azimuth traits identified several candidate genes associated with auxin signaling, which is expected to regulate phyllotaxy.

papers.abstract_full: The genetic architecture of obesity is highly polygenic. Recent genomic analyses have demonstrated that the heritability of Body Mass Index (BMI) is largely recovered when the full spectrum of common and rare variants is considered. Therefore, the challenge for the field is no longer a "missing heritability" gap. The challenge is a lack of mechanistic resolution: mapping genetic variants to specific physiological pathways. This paper proposes that supplementing BMI with mass-flux endophenotypes can achieve this resolution. I introduce three endophenotypes grounded in the Mass Balance Model (MBM). The primary endophenotypes are 24-hour urinary nitrogen excretion (nitrogen mass balance) and the respiratory quotient (substrate oxidation). The mass-clearance parameter k is introduced as an exploratory, biophysical measure of clearance efficiency. Reinterpreting canonical obesity genes (FTO, MC4R, leptin) through this framework reveals that they likely govern specific aspects of macronutrient partitioning. I acknowledge the dominant functional genomics at the FTO locus (IRX3/IRX5 enhancers) and the primary role of leptin in human appetite regulation (NMI). I outline a targeted research program using metabolic chamber studies, integrated with biobank data, to test these endophenotypes.

I outline a targeted research program using metabolic chamber studies, integrated with biobank data, to test these endophenotypes.

papers.title: Excluded causal variants produce false discoveries in genetic fine-mapping
papers.abstract: Statistical fine-mapping seeks to distinguish causal genetic variants from correlated variants in linkage disequilibrium (LD). Although fine-mapping algorithms perform well in simulations, they are often applied in settings that violate their assumptions. papers.abstract_full: Statistical fine-mapping seeks to distinguish causal genetic variants from correlated variants in linkage disequilibrium (LD). Although fine-mapping algorithms perform well in simulations, they are often applied in settings that violate their assumptions. In particular, genome-wide association study (GWAS) and quantitative trait locus (QTL) workflows routinely omit variants with minor allele frequency (MAf) below 1% and most insertions and deletions (indels), excluding many causal variants before fine-mapping begins. To assess this empirically, we compared filtered and unfiltered fine-mapping at 499 All of Us loci. Twenty percent of high-confidence calls after a 1% MAf filter, and 32% when indels were also omitted, lacked support in the unfiltered analysis. Errors were particularly enriched when tested variants tagged an omitted variant, so fine-mapping misassigned its signal to a proxy variant. At  RBO , omitting the frameshift that defines blood group O gave near-certain posterior inclusion probabilities (PIPs) to linked single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). To address this disconnect, we developed SuSiE-OUT, which enables fine-mapping in scenarios with possibly omitted causal variants. Modeling infinitesimal effects did not reliably prevent these errors, whereas imputing omitted variants or modeling them with our SuSiE-OUT method prevented most errors. Overall, we find that common analysis workflows substantially increase false discoveries in fine-mapping analyses, and we demonstrate two approaches to mitigate this challenge.

papers.abstract: Objectives  Bilateral and trilateral selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) aim to ensure symmetric hemispheric perfusion during aortic arch surgery, which current monitoring cannot directly assess. papers.abstract_full: Objectives  Bilateral and trilateral selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) aim to ensure symmetric hemispheric perfusion during aortic arch surgery, which current monitoring cannot directly assess. As a step towards real-time monitoring, we assessed the feasibility of multichannel contrast-enhanced near-infrared spectroscopy (CE-NIRS) using indocyanine green and whether hemispheric bolus timing matched expectations for each perfusion configuration. Methods  In this prospective, offline-analysed pilot study, 10 patients undergoing aortic arch surgery (9 frozen elephant trunk) received 94 boluses across 10 perfusion configurations. The interhemispheric difference in time to peak (ΔTTP) was compared with the pre-bypass baseline using a linear mixed model with Holm correction, alongside cerebral oximetry; the relationship to postoperative cerebral injury was explored post hoc. Results  92 of 94 boluses yielded a bilateral TTP. Contrary to expectation, the left hemisphere peaked later under bilateral (+7.2 s, 95% CI 3.4–11.0; p = 0.003) and trilateral SACP (+8.7 s, 2.5–14.8; p = 0.031). With both left-sided arch vessels on body perfusion, the asymmetry reversed (−7.0 s, −11.7 to −2.3; p = 0.025). ΔTTP detected 6 of 9 configuration effects, whereas oximetry detected none after correction. The three patients with cerebral injury showed the three most pronounced reversals (exact p = 0.100) but were also those managed trilaterally. Conclusions  Multichannel CE-NIRS is feasible during aortic arch surgery, without indicator-related adverse events. Bilateral and trilateral SACP did not secure symmetric indicator delivery; the configuration-dependent asymmetry and its reversal point to two steals within the perfusion circuit that oximetry missed. Their clinical relevance requires prospective confirmation.

papers.abstract: Abstract    Background  This study aimed to investigate the shared genetic etiology between gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, and to identify shared genomic loci, genes, and pathways.​  Methods  Using aggregated genome-wide association statistics from public data sources, a genome-wide pleiotropic association study was conducted. Multiple statistical genetic approaches were applied to sequentially explore pleiotropic associations across genome-wide single-nucleotide variations,…
papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Background  This study aimed to investigate the shared genetic etiology between gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, and to identify shared genomic loci, genes, and pathways.​  Methods  Using aggregated genome-wide association statistics from public data sources, a genome-wide pleiotropic association study was conducted. Multiple statistical genetic approaches were applied to sequentially explore pleiotropic associations across genome-wide single-nucleotide variations, genes, biological pathways, and gut microbiota. The potential shared genetic causes among 7 gastrointestinal tract diseases and 11 cardiovascular diseases were analyzed.​  Results  A total of 350 pleiotropic loci were identified. Colocalization analysis detected 95 shared causal loci across disease pairs. Multiple gene pathways were found to be closely associated with these diseases, and key biological processes—including cell signal transduction and T-cell activation—exhibited significant correlations across the studied diseases. A robust pleiotropic association was observed between gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, suggesting that these diseases may cross-influence each other in the context of different immune cells and tissues, while sharing common immune response mechanisms. Several immune cell populations, such as CD103⁺ CD11b⁺ dendritic cells, CD8⁺ splenic lymph node DCs, and γδ T cells, showed cross-disease correlations, highlighting the critical role of the immune system in the pathogenesis of both gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases. Multitrait colocalization analysis via HyPrColoc identified 6 pleiotropic loci harboring shared microbiota, underscoring the significant involvement of gut microbiota in disease pleiotropy.​  Conclusions  This study establishes a genetic and mechanistic framework for the shared etiology of gastrointestinal tract and cardiovascular diseases, with pleiotropic variants, inflammatory pathways, and gut microbiota interactions as key drivers. These insights not only deepen our understanding of cardiovascular-gastrointestinal comorbidities but also lay the groundwork for precision medicine strategies targeting shared biological mechanisms.

papers.abstract_full: ABSTRACT  Background  Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently co-occur, but the contributions of shared genetic susceptibility and directional associations remain unclear. Methods  We analyzed European-ancestry GWAS summary statistics for ADHD (38,691 cases; 186,843 controls) and BPD (12,339 cases; 1,041,717 controls). Linkage disequilibrium score regression, conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), MR-LAP, CAUSE, colocalization, and SuSiE fine-mapping assessed genetic overlap and directional associations. Results  ADHD and BPD showed substantial genetic correlation (r_g = 0.733). ConjFDR identified 48 shared loci, of which 36 (75%) showed consistent effect directions across independent phenotype-specific comparisons. Functional annotation highlighted axon guidance, oxidative phosphorylation, and a developing midbrain cell-type signature. ADHD-to-BPD MR supported a positive association (22 instruments; IVW-β = 0.487, SE = 0.082, p = 3.27 × 10⁻⁹), persisting after outlier removal, MR-LAP correction, and exclusion of two instruments indexing colocalized loci. Reverse MR was also positive (five instruments; IVW-β = 0.303, SE = 0.112, p = 6.83 × 10⁻³), but showed heterogeneity and sensitivity to individual variants. CAUSE favored directional over sharing-only models for ADHD-to-BPD (ΔELPD = 6.98; p = 7.3 × 10⁻⁸) and BPD-to-ADHD (ΔELPD = 5.92; p = 6.2 × 10⁻⁵). Colocalization and SuSiE supported shared signals at loci indexed by rs17576773 and rs9969232 for ADHD-to-BPD and rs4727799 in the reverse direction. Conclusions  ADHD and BPD share extensive genetic susceptibility. Although CAUSE favored directional models in both directions, evidence across MR approaches was more consistent for ADHD-to-BPD. Shared genetic mechanisms and residual pleiotropy limit causal interpretation.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  The methods utilized to analyze genotype-by-environment interaction (GEI) and assess the yield stability of crop varieties are constantly evolving, favoring integrated multi-method analytical frameworks. In this study, an integrated BLUP-AMMI-WAASB-MTSI framework was deployed to evaluate kernel yield (KY) stability and multi-trait performance in maize. Ten genotypes (nine elite experimental hybrids and one commercial check, CHK) were evaluated in a randomized complete block design across 18 environments (nine locations over two cropping seasons). Combined analysis of variance revealed significant effects for location, genotype, and spatio-temporal interactions (LG and YLG) on KY. AMMI analysis decomposed the multiplicative interaction into four significant interaction principal components (IPCs), explaining 81.70% of the total GEI variation. Under the mixed-model (REML/BLUP) framework, high genotypic mean heritability (0.69) and selective accuracy (0.83) were achieved. According to the WAASB quadrant biplot and WAASBY superiority index (50:50 yield: stability weighting), hybrids H2, H3, and H1 combined top-tier predicted BLUP yields (13.35, 12.95, and 12.80 t ha-1) with broad environmental stability, outperforming the check cultivar (CHK: 12.65 t ha-1). For multi-trait selection across 10 traits, exploratory factor analysis (FA) partitioned the traits into four dimensions. Based on the multi-trait stability index (MTSI) at a 30% selection intensity, hybrids H2, H6, and H3 were selected as ideal ideotypes, achieving positive genetic gains for KY (+3.91%) and grain-filling duration (+2.20%), alongside desirable reductions in plant height (-1.55%) and ear height (-0.47%) for lodging resistance. Overall, hybrids H2 and H3 were identified as consensus elite germplasm for commercial deployment.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Late blight of potato (  Phytophthora infestans  ) remains a persistent threat to global potato production. Due to the pathogen’s ability to rapidly overcome race-specific resistance genes, modern potato breeding must focus on durable quantitative resistance, including the use of genomic selection approaches. In this study, several genomic prediction models for late blight resistance were evaluated, differing in their treatment of spatial effects and incorporation of indirect genetic effects (IGEs) from neighbors. The optimal model was subsequently extended to a bivariate formulation to derive maturity-corrected genomic breeding values, effectively removing the confounding influence of foliage maturity on late blight resistance. Our results showed that additive genetic variance for late blight resistance accounted for a substantial proportion of total variance (h² = 0.32±0.02) and IGEs from neighboring plots were significant based on a standard likelihood ratio test. Although IGEs explained only a small portion of total variances, their inclusion markedly improved model prediction accuracy. We also observed a relatively high genetic correlation between foliage maturity and late blight score (0.56± 0.09), indicating that late-maturing lines tend to exhibit higher levels of durable resistance to late blight. After correcting for the confounding influence of foliage maturity, the narrow-sense heritability of the residual breeding value remained moderate (h² = 0.26), suggesting that meaningful genetic gain through selection is still possible. From a breeder’s perspective, selection based on total late blight resistance could unintentionally favor late-maturing genotypes, due to the positive genetic correlation between two traits. However, with residual breeding value, it is possible to get a response to selection for late blight resistance without affecting foliage maturity type.

papers.abstract_full: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet  trans -QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce  TransMap , a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale  trans -QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual  trans -eGenes,  TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings,  TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher  trans -QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied  TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average  N= 476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of  TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average  N= 307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532  trans -regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with  cis -eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate  cis–trans–biomarker regulatory configurations.  TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal  cis -regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial  trans -regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified  trans -regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a  KNOP1 cis -eQTL associated in  trans with a microglial regulatory program containing  MS4A4E , with additional support from statistical mediation analysis.  TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of  trans -regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

papers.abstract_full: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analysed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4⁺ T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of  RGS5 . Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher  TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower  GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher  MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.
