papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Digital therapeutics (DTx) are evidence-based software interventions with potential to complement conventional care; however, their adoption across European healthcare systems remains limited. Evidence on patient-level drivers, barriers, and implementation requirements is still scarce, especially regarding awareness, usability, reimbursement, and stakeholder engagement. METHODS: This mixed-methods study combined an online survey in five European countries - the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, and Spain - with a qualitative advisory board. Of 915 survey respondents, 682 surveys were included. Respondents were adults who had visited a healthcare professional in the previous 12 months. Survey findings were complemented by an advisory board involving 13 opinion leaders, patient experts, representatives of patient organizations, and industry professionals. RESULTS: Awareness and prior use of DTx were limited: 51.03% of respondents were unaware of DTx before the survey, while only 3.40% had previously used DTx. Nevertheless, 63.20% expressed interest in using DTx to better manage their condition. The main drivers of adoption were interest in testing tools (35.63%), physician recommendation (35.48%), 24/7 access to support (26.54%), nurse recommendation (19.21%), and additional support beyond conventional treatments (15.10%). Integration with wearables or health apps (52.49%) and involvement of patients or patient organizations in development (47.65%) further increased willingness to use DTx. Major barriers were lack of awareness (31.52%), doubts about effectiveness (21.11%), high out-of-pocket costs (19.50%), perceived complexity (16.72%), low motivation (15.54%), and data privacy concerns (15.25%). Advisory board participants identified education, trust-building, patient co-design, clinical endorsement, workflow integration, reimbursement clarity, and multidisciplinary ecosystem development as critical enablers. CONCLUSIONS: DTx adoption in Europe is constrained less by lack of interest than by limited awareness, trust, usability, evidence perception, and reimbursement uncertainty. Implementation will require patient-centered design, structured education for patients and healthcare professionals, transparent evidence generation, integration into clinical workflows, and harmonized regulatory and reimbursement pathways.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: To systematically evaluate adverse event reporting patterns and potential safety signals associated with resmetirom using the U.S. Food and Drug Administration Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). METHODS: FAERS reports from the first quarter of 2024 through the second quarter of 2026 were analyzed. Adverse events associated with resmetirom were coded using the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities and evaluated at the Preferred Term (PT) and System Organ Class (SOC) levels. Signal detection was performed using the reporting odds ratio, proportional reporting ratio, Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network, and Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker. A signal was considered positive only when all 4 algorithms met their predefined criteria. Time-to-onset patterns were further assessed using Weibull distribution analysis. RESULTS: A total of 2035 resmetirom-related reports were identified. The most frequently reported adverse events included diarrhea, nausea, pruritus, fatigue, and increased alanine aminotransferase. Positive PT-level signals were observed across gastrointestinal, hepatobiliary, laboratory, and thyroid-related events, including diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, hepatotoxicity, suspected drug-induced liver injury, cholelithiasis, and abnormalities in thyroid function tests. At the SOC level, investigations and hepatobiliary disorders met all 4 signal detection criteria. Among 220 reports with valid onset information, the median time to onset was 14.5 days (interquartile range, 1.5-60.5 days). The Weibull shape parameter was 0.60 (95% CI, 0.54-0.67), indicating an early failure pattern. CONCLUSIONS: This postmarketing pharmacovigilance study largely reinforced the known gastrointestinal, hepatic, gallbladder, and thyroid-related safety profile of resmetirom while identifying additional reporting signals that warrant further investigation. Adverse events tended to be reported early after treatment initiation, supporting closer monitoring during the initial treatment period. These findings should be interpreted as disproportionality signals rather than evidence of incidence or causality and require validation in longitudinal real-world studies.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Allergic rhinitis (AR) is a common chronic inflammatory disease characterized by dysregulated immune responses and pronounced circadian rhythm disturbances. However, the molecular mechanisms linking circadian rhythm-related genes (CRRGs) to AR pathogenesis and immune heterogeneity remain insufficiently understood. METHODS: Public microarray datasets (GSE75011 and GSE43523) were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between AR patients and healthy controls were identified using the limma package. Circadian rhythm-related DEGs (DECRRGs) were obtained by intersecting DEGs with curated CRRGs. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to identify AR-related gene modules. Machine learning algorithms, including support vector machine-recursive feature elimination and Boruta, were used to screen diagnostic biomarkers. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT and single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis. Single-gene gene set enrichment analysis, non-negative matrix factorization-based molecular subtyping, and competing endogenous RNA (ceRNA) network construction were subsequently performed. RESULTS: A total of 36 DECRRGs were identified and significantly enriched in immune- and inflammation-related pathways. WGCNA revealed a turquoise module that was strongly correlated with AR. Machine learning analysis identified two key diagnostic biomarkers, BTG1 and IDI1, which demonstrated robust diagnostic performance in both the training set (AUC = 0.781 and 0.755) and the validation set (AUC = 0.986 and 0.857). Immune infiltration analysis revealed significant alterations in immune cell composition between AR and control samples. Non-negative matrix factorization clustering classified AR patients into two distinct molecular subtypes with markedly different immune landscapes. Finally, a ceRNA regulatory network was constructed to elucidate the post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms of the diagnostic genes. CONCLUSIONS: This study systematically identified circadian rhythm-related diagnostic biomarkers for AR and revealed immune-based molecular subtypes, providing novel insights into the circadian-immune regulatory mechanisms underlying AR pathogenesis.

papers.abstract_full: TOPIC: How do the European Union (EU) Medical Device Regulation (MDR) (Regulation [EU] 2017/745) and the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) (Regulation [EU] 2024/1689) jointly regulate artificial intelligence (AI)‑enabled ophthalmic medical devices, and what are the implications for device classification, regulatory compliance, and clinical implementation? CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Artificial intelligence‑enabled ophthalmic medical devices, particularly Software as a Medical Device, are increasingly used for screening, diagnosis, and management of diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. As these technologies enter routine practice, understanding the complementary requirements of the MDR and AI Act is essential for ensuring patient safety, regulatory compliance, and trustworthy AI implementation. METHODS: This narrative review synthesizes peer-reviewed literature, EU legislation, regulatory guidance, and policy reports on AI-enabled ophthalmic medical devices. Evidence from major scientific databases and official EU sources was reviewed thematically to examine device classification, conformity assessment, high-risk AI requirements, transparency, postmarket surveillance, and emerging regulatory challenges. RESULTS: Most AI-enabled ophthalmic medical devices are classified as Class IIa, IIb, or III under the MDR and require notified body conformity assessment before Conformité Européenne marking. Under Article 6 of the AI Act, many also qualify as high-risk AI systems because they are safety components of MDR-regulated devices requiring third-party assessment. Manufacturers must, therefore, comply with both regulations, including requirements for risk management, data governance, technical documentation, transparency, human oversight, robustness, cybersecurity, and postmarket monitoring throughout the AI lifecycle. The implementation of the European Database on Medical Devices is expected to further strengthen regulatory transparency and postmarket oversight. CONCLUSIONS: The MDR and AI Act establish a complementary regulatory framework that combines medical device safety requirements with AI-specific governance. This review clarifies their interaction and provides practical guidance for clinicians, manufacturers, researchers, and regulators involved in the development, evaluation, and implementation of ophthalmic AI in Europe. FINANCIAL DISCLOSURES: Proprietary or commercial disclosure may be found in the Footnotes and Disclosures at the end of this article.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Coronary heart disease (CHD) remains the leading cause of global cardiovascular mortality. T cell-mediated adaptive immunity, particularly Th1, regulatory T cell (Treg), and Th17 subsets, plays a pivotal role in atherosclerotic plaque formation and destabilisation, yet a systematic, quantitative mapping of this research landscape is lacking. METHODS: Publications on T cell immunity in CHD from 1991 to August 2026 were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, restricted to English-language original articles. Bibliometric indicators were analysed with Microsoft Excel, VOSviewer (v1.6.20), CiteSpace (v6.4.R1), and bibliometric.com. Co-authorship, keyword co-occurrence, and burst-keyword analyses were performed. RESULTS: A total of 761 articles from 5,796 authors across 58 countries/regions and 299 journals were identified. Annual output increased markedly after 2010. China contributed the largest number of articles (n = 255, 33.5%), while the USA led in total citations (n = 8552), followed by China (n = 6,965) and Germany (n = 4,110). The most prolific and most highly cited author was Hansson Goran K. (14 publications; H-index = 13), while Becker AE achieved the highest average citation impact (248.0 citations per article). Circulation (IF = 35.5) was the leading journal by both article count (n = 33) and citations (n = 2,725). Keyword clustering revealed eight major research themes: clinical translation and computational approaches, T cell activation and immune cell interactions, classic immunopathology and plaque biology, inflammation and infectious triggers, Treg biology and T helper subsets, cytokine regulation and apoptosis, plaque vulnerability and ACS, and antigen presentation and extracellular vesicles. Burst analysis identified "machine learning", "monocytes", and "risk" as the most prominent emerging topics since 2023. CONCLUSION: Research on T cell immunity in CHD has grown markedly, with a clear shift toward the macrophage-T cell immune axis and immune-metabolic interactions, together with Treg-based therapeutic strategies and machine learning-assisted risk stratification. These findings provide a descriptive map that may help inform future translational research.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied across nephrology, with potential applications spanning disease prediction, diagnosis, treatment optimisation, and clinical decision support. However, reported model performance varies substantially across clinical domains, and high predictive performance does not necessarily demonstrate clinical utility or readiness for deployment. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on the applications of AI in nephrology and critically evaluates the methodological maturity, validation, interpretability, fairness, and translational readiness of AI systems across major nephrology domains. METHODS: A structured literature search of PubMed was conducted using terms related to AI and nephrology, with the primary eligibility period restricted to studies published from 2020 to 2025. The search strategy incorporated artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, natural language processing, large language models, generative AI, computer vision, reinforcement learning, federated learning, and related terms, together with nephrology and kidney-disease terms. Title/abstract and full-text screening were performed independently by the first and second authors, with disagreements resolved by the third author. Two foundational pre-2020 studies identified through citation chaining were retained because of their importance to the subsequent development of AI applications in nephrology. Evidence was synthesized qualitatively according to study design, validation, predictive performance, interpretability, fairness, prospective evaluation, and translational readiness. RESULTS: AI applications were identified across acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, nephropathology, kidney transplantation, haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, large language models, reinforcement learning, and federated learning. Across these domains, many models demonstrated promising discrimination, but evidence maturity varied considerably. External validation was present for some applications, whereas prospective evaluation and evidence of clinical utility remained limited. The literature also highlighted challenges related to calibration, generalizability, interpretability, algorithmic fairness, data governance, and integration into clinical workflows. Large language models and federated learning represent emerging areas, but nephrology-specific evidence remains comparatively limited. CONCLUSIONS: AI has substantial potential to support precision nephrology, but technical performance should not be equated with clinical effectiveness or deployment readiness. Future research should prioritize external and prospective validation, assessment of clinical utility and patient outcomes, transparent reporting, fairness, regulatory oversight, and effective human-AI integration.

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Pancreatic cancer (PC) remains a highly lethal malignancy due to asymptomatic progression, late presentation, and lack of reliable minimally invasive liquid biopsy biomarkers for early detection. Circulating microRNAs (c-miRNAs) are promising clinical indicators owing to their stability in body fluids and regulatory influence on oncogenic pathways. METHODS: This study presents an integrated computational framework combining large-scale serum miRNA expression profiling with differential expression analysis, machine learning (ML), and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Five publicly available GEO datasets comprising 1,101 serum samples were analyzed through preprocessing, including normalization, missing-value imputation, and ComBat-based batch correction. A Bayesian stacked ensemble classifier integrating XGBoost, Random Forest, SVC, Naïve Bayes, and k-NN was optimized using SMOTE for class imbalance and constrained weight minimization via SLSQP. RESULTS: Gene expression analysis identified 148 significantly dysregulated miRNAs (|log2FC| ≥ 2, adj. p < 0.05). The model achieved excellent predictive performance (AUC = 0.97; accuracy = 97.28%; sensitivity = 94%; specificity = 99%). SHAP-based XAI interpretation highlighted 20 miRNAs as the most influential predictors, including hsa-miR-125a-3p, hsa-miR-1290, hsa-miR-614, and hsa-miR-497-5p. Pathway enrichment using DIANA-miRPath and miRDB confirmed their involvement in key oncogenic pathways (MAPK, CDK, TP53). DISCUSSION: As a retrospective computational study, these findings represent computationally prioritized candidate biomarkers requiring validation in independent external cohorts and experimental approaches before clinical application. The proposed pipeline demonstrates a transparent, reproducible approach for biomarker discovery and validates the clinical promise of circulating miRNAs in minimally invasive liquid biopsy-based early detection of pancreatic cancer.

papers.abstract_full: Self-assembling peptide hydrogels (SAPHs) have emerged as promising platforms for mucosal drug delivery due to their excellent biocompatibility, programmable sequence design, and diverse triggering strategies. This review systematically discusses the molecular basis, synthesis techniques, and triggering strategies of SAPHs, highlighting how these elements collectively enable in situ gelation and on-demand drug release at mucosal sites. We also review applications across the oral, gastrointestinal, ocular, vaginal, middle ear, and respiratory mucosa, demonstrating the therapeutic potential of SAPHs in infection treatment, tissue repair, and immunomodulation. We further compare SAPHs with other mucosal delivery systems and summarize the clinical status of mucosal delivery products; although several products are in clinical use, no SAPH-based product has been approved for mucosal delivery, and the factors limiting clinical translation are discussed. Despite significant progress, several challenges remain, including balancing mechanical stability with degradation, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, confirming long-term biosafety, and obtaining regulatory approval. With the integration of artificial intelligence-assisted design and modular programmable platforms, SAPHs hold considerable promise for precision mucosal drug delivery.

papers.abstract: With the continuous expansion of cross-border agricultural supply chains, reliable food-safety risk screening under decentralized data ownership, heterogeneous sensing equipment, and jurisdiction-dependent, non-stationary regulatory limits pose a fundamental challenge to intelligent inspection systems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted regulation-aware heterogeneous multimodal federated learning framework that establishes a three-tier decoupling architecture. Firs…
papers.abstract_full: With the continuous expansion of cross-border agricultural supply chains, reliable food-safety risk screening under decentralized data ownership, heterogeneous sensing equipment, and jurisdiction-dependent, non-stationary regulatory limits pose a fundamental challenge to intelligent inspection systems. To address these limitations, this paper proposes an LLM-assisted regulation-aware heterogeneous multimodal federated learning framework that establishes a three-tier decoupling architecture. First, an available-modality and quality-adaptive fusion mechanism dynamically weights RGB images, near-infrared (NIR) spectra, and environmental time-series while enforcing strict zero weighting on unavailable modalities and continuous suppression of degraded observations. Second, a regulation-independent state-prototype collaboration and personalized federated learning strategy is developed on a unified continuous concentration scale, enabling cross-institutional transfer of physical contamination representations while avoiding the use of jurisdiction-dependent compliance labels to define shared prototype groups and preserving client-specific adapters against non-IID drift. Third, offline large language model (LLM) parsing transforms unstructured multi-jurisdictional trade regulations into machine-executable rule bases, which are coupled with an uncertainty-aware risk calibration module to dynamically determine exceedance probabilities and reinspection recommendations without retraining front-end sensing encoders when regulatory standards shift. Experimental evaluations on a multisource maize and aflatoxin B1 screening dataset in a workstation-based federated simulation demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.054±0.002 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.078±0.003, while elevating the area under the curve (AUC) and F1-score to 0.862±0.008 and 0.833±0.009, respectively, reducing the false negative rate (FNR) to 0.121±0.007 (p<0.001). Under severe client heterogeneity and missing-modality scenarios, the proposed approach maintains an AUC of 0.823±0.010 and an F1-score of 0.796±0.011. Ablation and ownership-level analyses assess robustness, calibration (expected calibration error of 0.032), and regulatory adaptation with fixed sensing encoders, providing an end-to-end, traceable decision-support paradigm for international agricultural trade screening.

papers.abstract_full: Anemia of inflammation (AI) is largely driven by interleukin-6 (IL-6)-induced hepcidin overproduction, which disrupts systemic iron homeostasis. Buteae monospermae Semen (BMS), the seeds of Butea monosperma (Lam.) Kuntze and a traditional Tibetan medicine, has long been used for blood-related disorders, yet its active constituents against AI remain unclear. Here, an integrated strategy combining ADMET screening, network pharmacology, deep learning-based affinity prediction, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, and in vitro validation was applied to 58 BMS-derived compounds. Forty-three candidates with acceptable ADMET profiles were retained, and their predicted targets were enriched in inflammation- and iron metabolism-related pathways, particularly IL-6/JAK2/STAT3 signaling. Two phenylpropanoid amides, compounds 16 and 21, were prioritized and shown to interact favorably with hepcidin-related regulatory targets. In IL-6-stimulated HepG2 cells, both compounds dose-dependently reduced hepcidin levels (EC50 = 2.486 and 14.49 μM), with therapeutic indices of 4.40 and 33.7, respectively. These findings identify BMS-derived phenylpropanoid amides as hepcidin-modulating candidates for AI and demonstrate an effective computational-experimental strategy for discovering bioactive compounds from traditional medicines.

papers.title: The Complexity and Fuzziness of Conformational Chemistry: Theory and Applications.
papers.abstract: Molecular structure is traditionally described in terms of chemical composition, atomic connectivity, and three-dimensional geometry. However, many molecules, particularly biomacromolecules, exist not as single structures but as dynamic ensembles of interconverting conformers whose populations depend on the surrounding physicochemical context. This work proposes that such conformational ensembles can be interpreted as molecular fuzzy sets, thereby establishing a conceptual bridge between conform…
papers.abstract_full: Molecular structure is traditionally described in terms of chemical composition, atomic connectivity, and three-dimensional geometry. However, many molecules, particularly biomacromolecules, exist not as single structures but as dynamic ensembles of interconverting conformers whose populations depend on the surrounding physicochemical context. This work proposes that such conformational ensembles can be interpreted as molecular fuzzy sets, thereby establishing a conceptual bridge between conformational chemistry, information theory, and fuzzy logic. The theoretical framework is introduced by representing molecular structures as adjacency matrices and extending this description to conformational distributions. Experimental evidence is discussed through the photochromic behavior of merocyanines, whose temperature- and environment-dependent conformational distributions encode measurable amounts of fuzzy information. Further support is provided by proteins, DNA, and RNA, where conformational heterogeneity underlies multifunctionality, gene regulation, alternative splicing, molecular recognition, and adaptive cellular responses. Within this perspective, biological function emerges from context-dependent distributions of molecular states rather than from unique static structures. Conformational ensembles are also described as thermalized quantum mixed states, suggesting new links between molecular complexity, fuzzy information processing, and quantum biological phenomena. Finally, the implications of molecular fuzziness for Chemical Artificial Intelligence are discussed, highlighting the possibility of exploiting molecular conformational dynamics as a substrate for adaptive, context-sensitive, and chemically embodied information processing.

papers.abstract_full: Plant tissue culture is essential for clonal propagation, germplasm conservation, genetic transformation, and genome editing in woody plants, yet these species remain highly challenging in vitro due to developmental recalcitrance, phenolic oxidation, endogenous contamination, seasonal effects, hyperhydricity, rooting difficulty, and strong genotype dependence. Medium formulation is therefore often a decisive factor rather than a routine technical step. This review examines the development, composition, and application of tissue culture media for woody species, emphasizing how specialized formulations emerged to overcome limitations of general-purpose media such as Murashige and Skoog medium. Major woody-targeted media, including Woody Plant Medium, Quoirin and Lepoivre medium, Anderson's medium, Driver and Kuniyuki Walnut medium, Rugini Olive Medium, Litvay medium, and DCR medium, are discussed in relation to the physiological needs of their target species. Key medium components are reviewed, including mineral nutrients, carbon sources, vitamins, plant growth regulators, organic additives, gelling agents, and pH, with attention to nitrogen form, ionic strength, calcium supply, iron availability, and pathway-dependent plant growth regulator selection. The review further highlights applications in conservation, micropropagation, transformation, and genome editing, and discusses emerging approaches such as statistical optimization, machine learning, nanoparticles, temporary immersion systems, biostimulants, and morphogenic regulators.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, reproducibility, and efficiency in anatomical pathology, but technical success alone does not establish clinical utility. In this Perspective, we examine practical requirements for translating computational pathology tools into routine practice, including prioritization of genuine clinical bottlenecks, representative datasets, independent validation, workflow integration, costs, clinician oversight, regulatory complia…
papers.abstract_full: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, reproducibility, and efficiency in anatomical pathology, but technical success alone does not establish clinical utility. In this Perspective, we examine practical requirements for translating computational pathology tools into routine practice, including prioritization of genuine clinical bottlenecks, representative datasets, independent validation, workflow integration, costs, clinician oversight, regulatory compliance, and post-deployment monitoring. We distinguish evidence from retrospective model evaluations, controlled reader studies, prospective workflow assessments, and economic simulations, recognizing that their conclusions are not interchangeable. We also propose a staged, decision-oriented framework through which laboratories can assess clinical need, select technologies, perform local validation, conduct prospective pilots, deploy with safeguards, and monitor performance throughout the AI lifecycle. Evidence from selected applications is encouraging, but effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, and readiness for routine use vary by intended purpose and practice environment. Responsible adoption should therefore be guided by demonstrated clinical benefit, operational feasibility, and ongoing evaluation rather than algorithmic performance alone.

papers.abstract_full: Background: Digital mental health platforms increasingly deploy self-directed single-label mood tracking as an ecological momentary assessment (EMA) tool, often framed as a screening indicator for depression or anxiety. Whether such naturalistic mood logs accurately detect screening-positive PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores has not been tested at scale against validated Arabic-language reference-standard instruments. Objectives: To evaluate, retrospectively, how accurately naturalistic single-label Arabic mood tracking detects screening-positive scores on the validated Arabic PHQ-9 and Arabic GAD-7 administered on the same platform, and to characterise the convergent-validity signal on continuous scores. Methods: This was a retrospective linked-records study of a Saudi Arabic-language commercial digital mental health platform. From 25,555 adult mood-logging users (aged 18 years or older), we assembled three intersection cohorts: depression (n = 4236), anxiety (n = 2449), and both-scales (n = 1825). Nine Arabic mood labels were categorised a priori as negative, positive, or neutral. Operating characteristics with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals were computed for four primary indices; thirteen comparator specifications and four machine-learning models were compared against the best-performing index. AUC differences were evaluated with a DeLong-equivalent bootstrap test. Reporting followed STARD. Results: The best-performing index (proportion of negative logs) yielded an AUC of 0.624 (95% CI 0.604-0.642) for screening-positive detection of depression and 0.652 (0.629-0.676) for anxiety, both below the conventional 0.80 benchmark for a clinically useful screening test. Youden-optimal sensitivity and specificity were 0.522 (0.506-0.538) and 0.712 (0.679-0.741) for depression and 0.569 (0.547-0.589) and 0.706 (0.670-0.743) for anxiety. Positive likelihood ratios of 1.81 and 1.93 fell below the 2-5 range that is conventionally associated with even small clinically meaningful shifts in post-test probability. Current diagnostic reliance on high-sensitivity cardiac troponin dynamic monitoring introduces hazardous delays (4–6 hours detection window) and yields false negatives in 20% of non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Pericoronary adipose tissue attenuation index (FAI), quantifying vascular inflammation through computed tomography (CT) attenuation changes in pericoronary fat, offers mechanistic insight into coronary plaque destabilization. However, the translational pathway from this biomarker to clinically actionable decision support remains incompletely realized, particularly regarding integration with established anatomical and functional parameters and explicit clinical interpretability. Hypothesis: A mechanistically grounded, multi-dimensional nomogram combining FAI with coronary CT angiography (CCTA)-derived anatomical stenosis (%DS), left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and smoking status—rendered interpretable through SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)—would achieve robust ACS-SCAD discrimination while providing transparent, auditable decision logic suitable for clinical implementation. Methods: In this prospective diagnostic accuracy study adhering to TRIPOD 2019 guidelines, 388 patients (ACS 117 [30.2%], SCAD 271 [69.8%]) underwent CCTA with standardized FAI, %DS, and LVEF acquisition. Stratified randomization (7:3) produced training (n=271) and validation (n=117) sets with preserved outcome distribution. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression with 10-fold stratified cross-validation compared lambda.min versus lambda.1se selection criteria, followed by multivariable logistic regression. Performance was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, Brier score, and decision curve analysis. KernelSHAP parsed individualized decision contributions. Regulatory-readiness was evaluated through predetermined change control documentation and explanation stability assessment. Results: LASSO lambda.min retained %DS, FAI, LVEF, RVEF, and smoking; lambda.1se selected only %DS and FAI. Final model incorporated %DS, FAI, LVEF, and smoking based on mechanistic non-overlap (RVEF-LVEF functional redundancy) and epidemiological importance. papers.abstract: RNA foundation models with diverse architectures have shown promise for learning representations of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences. papers.abstract_full: RNA foundation models with diverse architectures have shown promise for learning representations of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences. However, existing benchmarks commonly reduce token-level embeddings to transcript-level representations through global mean pooling before fitting a downstream probe. This aggregation does not explicitly preserve the identities of biologically distinct mRNA regions. Consequently, signals associated with short regulatory regions may be diluted, confounding assessments of representation quality with the information preserved by the readout. We introduce an architecture-agnostic, region-aware readout that separately averages embeddings within the 5$'$ untranslated region (UTR), coding sequence, and 3$'$ UTR and concatenates the resulting representations for linear probing. We reproduce mRNABench evaluations for 20 frozen models from 18 families, with a median absolute score difference of 0.0009 across 380 model--dataset--target evaluations published for 19 models, and construct a region-aware benchmark using the same models, tasks, and splits. Relative to global mean pooling, region-aware pooling increases Pearson correlation, averaged across the 20 models, by 11--25\% on translation and stability tasks, with no statistically significant decreases detected for any model on the regression tasks. On classification tasks, relative changes in the area under the precision--recall curve range from $-3\%$ to $+11\%$. Boundary randomization and displacement generally reduce performance, while dimensionality-matched and sequence-composition controls indicate that the gains are not explained solely by increased feature dimensionality, region length, or guanine--cytosine (GC) content. Learned attention pooling approaches region-aware performance only when supplied with one query per region. In silico perturbations reveal stronger sensitivity to upstream AUGs (uAUGs) and their Kozak context, while analyses of endogenous transcripts show approximately threefold greater recovery of length- and GC-adjusted uAUG-associated differences than global-mean probes. Both readouts capture codon optimality. Model rankings averaged over the regression tasks remain largely stable, while within a task models move by several places. Our region-aware benchmark therefore provides a biologically structured and complementary evaluation of mRNA foundation models, revealing regulatory information that is less accessible to linear probes after global mean pooling. papers.abstract_full: Dynamic RNA-protein interactions influence RNA transport, storage, stability, and activity and are fundamental to a broad range of biological processes. During the oocyte-to-embryo transition (OET), fully differentiated gametes fuse and regain totipotency. Throughout the OET, the transcription remains silent. Spatiotemporal regulation of gene expression relies on the dynamic interactions between maternal transcripts and various protein complexes. Despite its fundamental importance, RNA-protein interaction dynamics at the global level during the OET remain poorly understood. Here, we leverage fractionation RNA-seq to profile RNA insolubility, a proxy for the interaction between RNAs and protein complexes, during zebrafish OET. We identify transcripts that transition between the soluble (relatively protein-free) and insoluble (heavily protein-associated) states and demonstrate that these phase transitions are driven by ribosome-dependent and ribosome-independent mechanisms. We demonstrate that the capacity of maternal RNAs to engage with protein complexes changes dynamically during the OET through remodeling of cis-regulatory features. We developed a machine-learning framework and uncovered multiple cis- and trans-regulatory features that may contribute to RNA insolubility. To validate these predictions, we examined poly(A) tail length and m6A dynamics. We found that poly(A) tail length is associated with both ribosome-dependent and ribosome-independent RNA phase transitions. In parallel, fractionation m6A-pulldown RNA-seq revealed highly dynamic changes in the m6A landscape during the OET. A correlation between m6A modifications and RNA insolubility is gradually established during the OET. Together, our findings uncover a multilayered regulatory mechanism governing RNA phase transitions during the OET, providing fundamental insights into post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression during development.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Accurate prediction of RNA-protein binding is essential for understanding post-transcriptional regulation, yet existing computational approaches typically aggregate features globally, which limits the spatial resolution required to map specific mechanistic determinants of binding. Here, we introduce GraPhiT-RBP, a protein-aware framework that employs graph-guided cross-attention to explicitly model relationships between RNA nucleotides and individual protein residues. By preserving molecular resolution during interaction learning, GraPhiT-RBP enables direct biological interpretation: it recovers experimentally characterized RNA-binding motifs, maps spatial attention directly to known RNA-binding domains, and predicts the disruptive effects of clinically annotated single-nucleotide variants. Evaluated across 261 transcriptome-wide datasets spanning six human cell lines, this architecture achieved superior predictive accuracy (mean AUC 0.9326) and robust zero-shot generalization to previously unseen proteins compared to eight established methods. Notably, GraPhiT-RBP extracts these transferable recognition features using 69% fewer trainable parameters than the strongest-performing baseline. Together, GraPhiT-RBP offers a highly generalizable, mechanistically interpretable framework for characterizing molecular recognition and investigating previously unexplored RNA-protein regulatory networks.

papers.abstract: RNA plays a critical and diverse role in gene expression, catalysis, regulation, and molecular recognition. This functional versatility arises from the interplay between nucleotide sequence, structural organization, and cellular context. papers.abstract_full: RNA plays a critical and diverse role in gene expression, catalysis, regulation, and molecular recognition. This functional versatility arises from the interplay between nucleotide sequence, structural organization, and cellular context. Nevertheless, most RNA foundation models are pretrained primarily using sequence or secondary-structure information, while the systematic integration of three-dimensional geometric and conformational features remains comparatively underexplored. Here, we introduce RNAtomy, a self-supervised RNA foundation model designed to learn the structural anatomy of RNA from inter-nucleotide geometry and residue-level conformational descriptors. Its design has three main components: 1) joint masked reconstruction of pairwise geometry and residue-level descriptors to connect spatial organization with local conformation; 2) a hybrid Mamba-Transformer backbone in which Mamba blocks efficiently propagate global context, while shifted-window attention compensates for the absence of explicit content-dependent token interactions in Mamba by modeling relationships within local regions of the pairwise map; and 3) axis-aware feature-wise linear modulation that maps nucleotide-level conformations to the row and column axes of pairwise geometry. We assess RNAtomy across seven diverse tasks involving structural and functional predictions at the nucleotide, nucleotide-pair, and RNA levels. RNAtomy achieved particularly strong performance on structural tasks, outperforming established RNA foundation models and task-specific approaches in contact and long-range base-pair prediction. Its representations also transferred effectively to interaction-related tasks, despite the substantial differences between these applications and the structural pretraining objective. On functional tasks, RNAtomy achieved superior performance in translation-related prediction and regulatory-element identification. Notably, RNAtomy achieved these results despite being pretrained on a substantially smaller training set than the RNA foundation models used as baselines. Together, these results highlight how rich structural information, when learned through an expressive architecture, can support transferable RNA representations across biologically distinct structural and functional applications.

papers.title: The Synthetic Other: A neurocognitive framework for AI companionship and dependence
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions can provide emotional support, but the availability, responsiveness, personalization, and affirmation that make them effective regulators may concentrate regulation within a single synthetic relationship. We propose a neurocognitive framework that situates AI companionship along a continuum from regulatory scaffolding to regulatory substitution, linking this transition to distributed systems supporting social-regulatory relief, motivational valuation, self…
papers.abstract_full: Artificial intelligence (AI) companions can provide emotional support, but the availability, responsiveness, personalization, and affirmation that make them effective regulators may concentrate regulation within a single synthetic relationship. We propose a neurocognitive framework that situates AI companionship along a continuum from regulatory scaffolding to regulatory substitution, linking this transition to distributed systems supporting social-regulatory relief, motivational valuation, self-AI representation, and behavioral control. At the core of the framework is synthetic companion dependence, defined by reduced regulatory substitutability: functions served by a particular companion become increasingly difficult to redistribute across alternative people, strategies, or contexts. We distinguish regulatory scaffolding, which preserves or expands a broader regulatory repertoire, from regulatory substitution, in which regulation becomes concentrated within the synthetic relationship. Regulatory centrality, diminished control, and disruption sensitivity are candidate markers of dependence, whereas persistent displacement or functional impairment marks maladaptiveness. The framework links social-regulatory relief, motivational valuation, self-AI representation, and behavioral control to distributed neurocognitive systems and predicts a progressive shift in the relative neural prioritization of the preferred companion over viable regulatory alternatives. It thereby shifts attention from use intensity to whether regulatory functions remain flexibly replaceable.

papers.abstract: Abstract  Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in decisions that affect health, safety, welfare and rights, and regulators have responded by requiring “control safeguards”, such as human oversight, robustness and monitoring, for systems classed as high-risk. This article asks why such safeguards are hard to implement and why the difficulty matters for society. It combines doctrinal analysis of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended in…
papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in decisions that affect health, safety, welfare and rights, and regulators have responded by requiring “control safeguards”, such as human oversight, robustness and monitoring, for systems classed as high-risk. This article asks why such safeguards are hard to implement and why the difficulty matters for society. It combines doctrinal analysis of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, as amended in 2026) with a structured critical review of the technical, human-factors and policy literature. Five technical barriers are identified (model opacity, speed and autonomy, brittle guardrails, limits of human attention and judgement, and the lack of tests for control effectiveness), together with six legal and institutional barriers (open-textured legal standards, uncertain classification, delayed standards and guidance, limited regulatory capacity, fragmented enforcement, and burdens on small organisations). The article argues that these barriers reinforce one another through three gaps: a feasibility gap between what the law demands and what technology can deliver, a verification gap between legal requirements and testable criteria, and a capacity gap between large and small actors and between providers and regulators. Mapping each oversight capability in Article 14(4) to these barriers shows where safeguards are most likely to be formal rather than effective. The article proposes ten recommendations for EU institutions, standard-setters, national authorities, providers and deployers, and considers lessons for lower-capacity jurisdictions, including in Africa, that are drawing on EU-style models. The central conclusion is that regulatory attention should shift from documenting oversight to demonstrating that it works.

papers.abstract_full: The placenta is a crucial determinant of the success of pregnancy. However, manual evaluation of its pathology is limited by poor reproducibility and a global shortage of specialized perinatal pathologists. Besides, predicting recurrent pregnancy complications remains highly challenging, which severely limits the timely deployment of proactive therapeutic interventions. Automated artificial intelligence screening of the delivered placenta will help to overcome these bottlenecks. In this work, we synthesize the transition toward self-supervised Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) that yield robust, stain-agnostic tissue embeddings. Furthermore, we evaluate the emergence of Non-Euclidean Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) that map cellular topologies to quantify mal-perfusion, alongside multimodal generative cross-attention networks (MGCN) that integrate gigapixel histology with electronic medical records (EMR) to improve pregnancy risk stratification. Moreover, we propose a novel, functional systems-biology framework to retroactively bridge digital morphometrics – such as impaired trophoblast fusion and invasion – to upstream dysregulated molecular cascades, including the ERK1/2–DUSP, FAK–MAPK, and HIF-1α regulatory axes. Finally, we address translational bottlenecks – such as diagnostic inter-observer variation, systemic clinical confounders, and geographic data bias – and outline hardware edge-deployment strategies for the pathology floor. Ultimately, automated placental screening will help to reveal immediate newborn developmental risks and maternal pathological recurrence risks across subsequent pregnancies. Together, these computational paradigms offer a potential translational roadmap to standardize digital placental pathology into a personalized reproductive medicine pillar.

papers.abstract: The gastrointestinal tract is a dynamic regulatory interface in which the enteric nervous system (ENS), supported by an extensive enteric glial cell (EGC) network, interacts with the enteric immune system (EIS) and gut microbiota to maintain epithelial barrier integrity, neuroplasticity, motility, and tissue repair. papers.abstract_full: The gastrointestinal tract is a dynamic regulatory interface in which the enteric nervous system (ENS), supported by an extensive enteric glial cell (EGC) network, interacts with the enteric immune system (EIS) and gut microbiota to maintain epithelial barrier integrity, neuroplasticity, motility, and tissue repair. In eubiosis, coordinated signaling across this tripartite axis supports intestinal homeostasis. Dysbiosis, however, can reduce short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) availability while increasing exposure to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), including lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and others. These changes may activate NF-κB and NLRP3 inflammasome signaling in enteric glial and immune cells, thereby promoting oxidative and nitrosative stress, neuronal hyperexcitability, apoptosis, barrier dysfunction, and local neuroinflammation, with possible consequences for gut–brain communication. This review examines the mechanisms through which dietary phytochemicals—including capsaicinoids, resveratrol, curcumin, catechins, quercetin, and sulforaphane—may modulate this ENS–EIS–microbiota axis. We focus on their actions at transient receptor potential channels, 5-hydroxytryptamine receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, SIRT1, and Nrf2-associated pathways, and their potential to limit inflammation, oxidative stress, and excitotoxic signaling. We also identify knowledge gaps and discuss future research and translational priorities, including human-relevant organoid models, spatial transcriptomics, and machine-learning-enabled multi-omics to define microbiota-derived metabolite–receptor interactions and guide personalized dietary strategies for enteric neuroglial health.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Surimi adulteration poses a significant challenge to food safety. This study developed a machine learning framework that uses 13 physicochemical and elemental features for fish category classification and adulteration-ratio prediction. Four models (RF, XGBoost, LightGBM, and MLP), with logistic regression and ridge regression baselines, were evaluated using 30 source composition records, simulated mixtures and 30 measured validation samples. Five outer record folds and three inner folds separated model selection from evaluation. Principal component analysis (PCA) and SHAP were applied for feature analysis and model interpretation. RF and LightGBM each correctly classified all 30 held-out source records. XGBoost showed the lowest mean internal regression RMSE (0.1061; R² = 0.8799). In the 30 measured validation samples at 0%, 30% and 50%, RF gave the numerically lowest validation error (MAE = 0.0542, RMSE = 0.0791, R² = 0.8517), while the internally selected XGBoost gave MAE = 0.0619, RMSE = 0.0792 and R² = 0.8515. This measured set was not used for model fitting, preprocessing, model selection or noise selection, but its sampling breadth is limited. SHAP analysis identified fat, moisture and zinc as prominent classification features and fat, iron and sodium as prominent regression features. These results support exploratory composition-based modelling; broader independent measured validation is still required for practical regulatory applications.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Background: Identifying which genes to perturb in order to drive a cell towards a desired state is a common problem in biology, and the answer is often a combination of genes. Single-cell foundation models can predict the effect of forcing a gene on without an experiment, but in silico perturbation has been confined to single genes or to a few hundred enumerated combinations. In token-based models, choosing which genes to force on is formally the same optimization problem as a discrete adversarial attack on a language model. We therefore investigated whether Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), a search developed for such attacks, can be used to find combinations of genes. Results: Our results suggest that GCG is useful for finding combinations of genes. In Geneformer, the effect of a set was well below the sum of the individual effects of its members, which suggests that assembling combinations from single-gene effects is not a promising approach. GCG exceeded forward-selection greedy search at equal cost in two models (Geneformer and scGPT) and at every set size. Against published reprogramming protocols, GCG recovered the reported factors at a rate well above chance and higher than the random-pool and all-gene greedy searches at equal cost, although ranking genes by their individual effect gave a higher recovery rate. Recovery corresponded to whether a search used the embedding gradient, which suggests that the gradient is useful for narrowing the search, whereas stronger optimization of the objective did not raise recovery, which suggests that the similarity induced by the model does not fully reflect the regulatory logic of genes. Conclusions: These results are obtained within the constraints of the foundation models; nevertheless, searching for combinations of factors with foundation models extends in silico perturbation beyond single genes, reveals a property of the induced objective that single-gene evaluation does not, and points to a new direction for using and evaluating the models.

papers.abstract: Abstract  Artificial intelligence agents—software systems that perceive, reason, plan and act over multiple steps with limited human intervention—are moving from research prototypes towards clinical deployment. papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Artificial intelligence agents—software systems that perceive, reason, plan and act over multiple steps with limited human intervention—are moving from research prototypes towards clinical deployment. Recent reviews map what has been built; this one asks what would have to hold for such systems to be deployed safely. We conducted a scoping review reported according to the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews, searching eight bibliographic sources from January 2017 to June 2026, admitting foundational computer science and regulatory literature alongside clinical applications. Five architectural paradigms recur—tool-augmented large language model agents, multi-agent systems, offline reinforcement learning agents, embodied robotic agents and autonomous monitoring agents—nearly all sharing a common four-layer stack. We introduce a six-level scale of clinical agent autonomy that grades systems by where human judgement enters relative to the reasoning, and by whether the resulting action remains reversible. The scale exposes an inversion in the evidence base: demonstrated patient benefit concentrates at high autonomy in narrow, bounded domains, whereas research effort concentrates at intermediate autonomy, where prospective outcome evidence is absent and automation bias is the dominant risk. We further propose seven evaluation dimensions specific to agency, a mapping of evaluation requirements to autonomy level, and a ten-item failure mode taxonomy assigned to the architectural layer at which each is addressable. Deploying agentic systems safely requires prospective multi-site validation, reporting standards adapted to agency, equity-aware design, and regulatory obligations indexed to autonomy rather than algorithm class. We conclude with an eight-point research agenda.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  The rapid digital transformation of higher education has increased dependence on cloud platforms, learning management systems, online assessment systems, research repositories, enterprise applications, and interconnected digital services. At the same time, this transformation has also considerably increased cyber risks facing higher education institutions (HEIs). Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) enables threat-intelligence analysis, security-log interpretation, anomaly investigation, incident-response assistance, and cybersecurity knowledge management. However, adoption brings challenges involving hallucination, privacy, organizational readiness, human oversight, accountability, regulatory compliance, and adversarial misuse. Existing cybersecurity and AI governance frameworks serve as foundational guidance, although they primarily concern cybersecurity risk management or AI governance independently and do not provide a holistic adoption framework explicitly focused on GenAI-based cybersecurity for HEI infrastructure. This paper presents a SWOT-based responsible adoption model composed of five aspects: GenAI cybersecurity capabilities, organizational readiness, ethical governance, regulatory compliance, and cybersecurity outcomes. A single comparative document analysis assesses the proposed framework with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0, NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) with its Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and higher-education cybersecurity guidance. This decision model utilizes nine evaluation criteria to review cybersecurity capability, GenAI specificity, organizational readiness, ethical governance, regulatory alignment, human oversight, higher-education contextualization, measurable cybersecurity outcomes, and implementation decision support. Results suggest that established frameworks offer robust but varying emphases of coverage, while the proposed model consolidates these concerns into an HEI-specific adoption decision layer. The framework aims to guide HEIs not only in understanding how GenAI can assist with cybersecurity, but also in determining whether the institution is prepared to apply it responsibly, what governance mechanisms should be established, and how its value can be evaluated.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract* Background Adaptive generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to personalize learning, yet evidence remains fragmented across system design, human–AI co-regulation, self-regulated learning (SRL), sustained behavioral outcomes, and ethics. This systematic scoping review mapped these dimensions in a single synthesis. Methods We searched Dimensions, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, Lens, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science on 5 May 2026. Of 3,084 records identified, 95 journal articles published between 2023 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Evidence was synthesized using descriptive mapping, form–function co-occurrence analysis, and qualitative comparative synthesis. Results Adaptive GenAI was most commonly instantiated as conversational tutors, generative content personalizers, and hybrid feedback systems, with adaptive feedback, content adaptation, diagnostic analysis, scaffolding, and progress tracking emerging as the dominant functions. Conceptualizations of human–AI co-adaptation were less mature: most studies framed AI primarily as a responsive regulator, with feedback-loop acceleration and metacognitive prompting more frequently articulated than internalization, behavioral reinforcement, or social modeling. Empirical effects were concentrated in proximal SRL outcomes, particularly forethought and performance, while evidence for self-reflection, affective regulation, transfer, stable self-efficacy, persistence, and learning habits was much thinner. Ethical evaluation likewise remained uneven, emphasizing feedback quality, pedagogical validity, well-being, autonomy, motivation, inclusivity, and agency, while transparency, data minimization, scaffold fading, developmental suitability, manipulation risk, and ethical nudging were addressed far less often. Conclusions Adaptive GenAI is more mature in technical personalization and proximal SRL support than in reciprocal co-regulation, durable behavior change, and integrated ethical governance. Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

Future research should test whether regulatory gains persist beyond immediate AI support and develop stronger frameworks for governing learner influence and dependency.

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly entering obstetrics and prenatal medicine, particularly in prenatal ultrasound, fetal echocardiography, fetal magnetic resonance imaging, genomic screening, risk prediction and clinical decision support. The aim of this review was to summarize current evidence, recent developments and implementation requirements for AI-based applications in prenatal care. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A structured narrative review was performed with emphasis on peer-reviewed and clinically relevant literature published from 2021 to 2026, supplemented by landmark methodological, regulatory and reporting guidance. Priority was given to systematic reviews, diagnostic accuracy studies, external validation studies, prospective evaluations, randomized educational or clinical studies, regulatory documents and reporting standards relevant to AI in medicine. RESULTS: The strongest current evidence supports AI-assisted standard-plane recognition, image-quality assessment and fetal biometry, followed by emerging applications in fetal cardiac screening, blind-sweep ultrasound, fetal MRI segmentation, placental phenotyping, prediction of fetal growth restriction, preterm birth and preeclampsia, and machine learning-enhanced cfDNA analysis. Generative and multimodal AI systems may support report drafting, guideline retrieval and education, but remain insufficiently validated for autonomous clinical decision-making. DISCUSSION: AI has the potential to improve access, standardization, efficiency and quality assurance in prenatal medicine. However, most applications remain limited by retrospective design, enriched datasets, insufficient external validation, unclear calibration, limited fairness analyses and incomplete workflow evaluation. Clinical adoption should therefore follow a human-in-the-loop model with prospective validation, transparent reporting, regulatory oversight, bias monitoring and post-market surveillance. AI should augment rather than replace specialist expertise in obstetrics and fetal medicine. EINLEITUNG: Künstliche Intelligenz (KI) findet zunehmend Eingang in die Geburtshilfe und Pränatalmedizin, insbesondere in den pränatalen Ultraschall, die fetale Echokardiografie und Magnetresonanztomografie, das genomische Screening, die Risikoprädiktion sowie die klinische Entscheidungsunterstützung. Ziel dieser Übersichtsarbeit war es, die aktuelle Evidenz, neuere Entwicklungen und die Voraussetzungen für die Implementierung KI-basierter Anwendungen in der Pränatalmedizin zusammenzufassen. MATERIAL UND METHODEN: Es wurde eine strukturierte narrative Literaturübersicht mit Schwerpunkt auf begutachteten und klinisch relevanten Publikationen aus den Jahren 2021 bis 2026 durchgeführt. Ergänzend wurden wegweisende methodische Arbeiten sowie regulatorische Vorgaben und Berichtsstandards berücksichtigt. Priorisiert wurden systematische Übersichtsarbeiten, Studien zur diagnostischen Genauigkeit, externe Validierungsstudien, prospektive Untersuchungen, randomisierte Ausbildungs- oder klinische Studien sowie regulatorische Dokumente und Berichtsstandards zur Anwendung von KI in der Medizin. ERGEBNISSE: Die derzeit belastbarste Evidenz besteht für die KI-gestützte Erkennung fetaler Standardschnittebenen, die Beurteilung der Bildqualität und die automatisierte fetale Biometrie. Weitere vielversprechende Anwendungsbereiche umfassen das Screening auf fetale Herzfehler, standardisierte Blind-Sweep-Ultraschallprotokolle, die Segmentierung fetaler MRT-Aufnahmen, die Charakterisierung der Plazenta, die Vorhersage fetaler Wachstumsrestriktion, von Frühgeburt und Präeklampsie sowie die durch maschinelles Lernen unterstützte Analyse zellfreier DNA. Generative und multimodale KI-Systeme können die Erstellung medizinischer Befunde, die leitlinienbasierte Informationsrecherche und die Aus- und Weiterbildung unterstützen, sind für eine autonome klinische Entscheidungsfindung bislang jedoch nicht ausreichend validiert. DISKUSSION: KI besitzt das Potenzial, den Zugang zur Pränatalmedizin zu verbessern sowie Standardisierung, Effizienz und Qualitätssicherung zu fördern. Die Aussagekraft vieler Anwendungen ist bislang jedoch durch retrospektive Studiendesigns, selektierte beziehungsweise angereicherte Datensätze, unzureichende externe Validierungen, eine unklare Kalibrierung, begrenzte Analysen möglicher Benachteiligungen einzelner Patientengruppen und eine unvollständige Evaluation im klinischen Arbeitsablauf eingeschränkt. Die klinische Einführung sollte daher einem Human-in-the-Loop-Modell folgen und eine prospektive Validierung, transparente Berichterstattung, regulatorische Kontrolle, kontinuierliches Bias-Monitoring sowie eine Überwachung nach der Markteinführung einschließen. KI sollte die fachärztliche Expertise in der Geburtshilfe und Fetalmedizin ergänzen, nicht ersetzen.

papers.abstract_full: INTRODUCTION: Synthetic biology is an emerging field that integrates engineering principles, molecular innovations, interdisciplinary methodologies, and designer toolkits to create versatile and adaptable platforms for control, enhance, and reprogram signaling, phenotype, or function in biological systems and living organisms. Advances in mammalian synthetic biology have generated growing interest in its translational applications, including cardiovascular drug discovery and disease management. AREAS COVERED: This concise report highlights promising synthetic biology-inspired technologies that have been applied or can potentially apply to transgene regulation and disease management in cardiovascular medicine, such as tunable regulatory switches, programmable gene circuits, synthetic sensing modules, and gut-heart axis engineering. We also summarize recent translational progress in the field and discuss remaining obstacles, potential solutions, and future opportunities, with particular emphasis on the progression from laboratory concepts to practical applications in cardiovascular disease. EXPERT OPINION: Synthetic biology is steadily advancing toward translation. However, barriers for clinical implementation remain, including non‑mammalian components, immunogenicity, regulatory uncertainty, and broader ethical and safety concerns. Emerging solutions, including humanized molecular components, advanced monitoring strategies, and machine learning, may help mitigate those risks and expand the cardiovascular utility of synthetic biology. Stronger evidence and deeper clinical integration will position the field for future cardiovascular medicine.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: To understand and improve long-term congenital heart surgery outcomes, longitudinal data are essential but challenging to capture. We evaluated a novel program to facilitate routine longitudinal data collection. METHODS: Patients undergoing Society of Thoracic Surgeons Benchmark Operations at two centers (2007-2019) were included. Annual follow-up data (vital status and age-specific burden of disease questionnaires) were collected using an automated email system along with medical record and local registry data queries, with coordinator follow-up if needed. Completeness of follow-up and associated factors were analyzed in multivariable logistic regression. RESULTS: Of 4,075 subjects, vital status was captured for 98% (median follow-up 6.0 years; IQR 3.1-9.2). Vital status at one year was known for 95%; overall follow-up completeness (observed-to-potential follow-up time) was 81%. At least one follow-up questionnaire was completed by 85%, with 58% utilizing the automated email system. Those with genetic/non-cardiac abnormalities (OR 2.28, 95%CI 1.28-4.28), single ventricle palliation (Norwood OR 11.2, 95%CI 3.01-72.7; Glenn/hemi-Fontan OR 7.79, 95%CI 2.21-49.5), and tetralogy of Fallot repair (OR 2.43, 95%CI 1.11-5.59) had higher odds of known vital status. Follow-up questionnaire completion had higher odds for non-Hispanic white patients (OR 1.54, 95%CI: 1.27-1.86) and higher median income households (OR 1.05/$10,000, 95%CI: 1.01-1.09). CONCLUSIONS: This program captured vital status and burden of disease, with one-year survival determined for nearly all patients. Automation reduced human resource needs by more than half. selected_papers.abstract_full: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a complex congenital heart disease (CHD) involving hypoplasia of the left ventricle (LV) and the aorta (Ao), along with aortic and mitral valve stenosis/atresia with or without coarctation. It is a physiologically single-ventricle lesion, previously uniformly fatal, but now survivable with a 3-stage surgical palliation ending with the Fontan circulation, a circulation for only one working ventricle. In the classical definition of HLHS, the ventricular septum is intact; however, HLHS variants have been described with similar single-ventricle pathophysiology in which the hypoplastic LV is not hemodynamically coupled to the aortic outflow. Evidence for a genetic etiology for HLHS is indicated by its high recurrence risk, the association with various chromosomal abnormalities, and the demonstration of mutations in mice causing HLHS. Despite surgical advances allowing survival of patients with HLHS, there is still high morbidity and mortality after their first-stage palliation. The causes of such high morbidity and mortality are not well understood, but most deaths are likely related to cardiovascular/hemodynamic causes. Studies in the animal models of HLHS show that this cardiac lesion arises early in embryogenesis, decreases left-sided inflow, and is associated with metabolic dysfunction, cell proliferation, and differentiation defects. Findings indicate HLHS is also associated with intrinsic cell deficits, deficits that may also contribute to the high risk of heart failure and adverse neurodevelopment. In this article, we update a previous review by describing the basic pathophysiology; pertinent pre- and postoperative management of HLHS and its anatomical variants; and novel insights from the HLHS mouse model on the causes of HLHS-associated heart failure and poor neurodevelopment, as well as potential therapeutic strategies.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is characterized by progressive ventricular dilation, systolic dysfunction, and an increased risk of arrythmias and sudden cardiac arrest. Variants in the LMNA gene, which encodes the nuclear lamins A and C, have been linked to the familial form of the disease and the founder variant p.Ser143Pro is particularly common among Finnish patients with DCM. To elucidate the complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms behind LMNA-related DCM, we generated a mouse model carrying the p.Ser143Pro mutation in the Lmna gene. All genetically modified mice appeared normal at birth. However, based on echocardiography, necropsy, natriuretic peptide B (Nppb) expression levels, and histopathological data, homozygous males developed progressive left ventricular dilatation, myocardial fibrosis, and cardiac failure after 6 months of age, with all succumbing before 10 months. A reduced disease penetrance was observed in heterozygous male and homozygous female mice, with one-year survival rates of 40% and 60%, respectively. No signs of skeletal myopathy were observed in mice carrying the mutation. Whole-transcriptome RNA sequencing analysis of left ventricular cardiac tissue from asymptomatic two-month-old homozygous male mice revealed an upregulation of classical heart failure markers, such as natriuretic peptide A (Nppa) and myosin heavy chain 7 (Myh7), and an elevated unfolded protein response signaling, as shown by elevated DNA damage inducible transcript 3 (Ddit3), BAG cochaperone 3 (Bag3) and CCAAT enhancer binding protein beta (Cebpb) levels. In conclusion, p.Ser143Pro-Lmna mice closely mimic the clinical phenotype observed in patients with the p.Ser143Pro LMNA variant and offer a valuable in vivo model for investigating the underlying pathogenic mechanisms of LMNA-related DCM. © 2026 The Author(s). selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is genetically heterogeneous. In severe non-ischemic DCM with familial clustering of heart-failure deaths, genetic testing and pedigree analysis may clarify etiology and guide cascade screening. CASE PRESENTATION: A 40-year-old woman presented with progressive dyspnea, chest tightness, and palpitations after an upper respiratory tract infection. Echocardiography showed severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction [left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) approximately 20%], left atrial enlargement, functional mitral regurgitation, and a small pericardial effusion. Serial cardiac troponin I and myocardial enzyme measurements remained within the reference ranges. Coronary angiography excluded obstructive coronary disease. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) demonstrated global left ventricular hypokinesis and a clinically reported non-ischemic late-gadolinium-enhancement pattern at the papillary-muscle level involving the anterior/lateral wall. Because cardiac biomarkers remained normal and dedicated inflammatory CMR sequences were not acquired, active myocarditis could not be confirmed. Guideline-directed therapy reduced NT-proBNP from 4154 to 828 pg/mL, although angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor therapy was limited by symptomatic hypotension. At 2 months, symptoms and daily activity tolerance improved, but LVEF remained 25%, QTc was 479 ms, and ventricular premature complexes persisted. Whole-exome sequencing identified heterozygous likely pathogenic variants in BAG3 (NM_004281.4:c.180 + 1G > T) and FLNC [NM_001458.5:c.761_779del, p.(Leu254Profs*14)]. The daughter carried the BAG3 variant, whereas both children were negative for FLNC. The proband reported heart-failure-related deaths in her father and younger brother during adulthood and in a nephew during childhood. CONCLUSIONS: The findings support complex familial non-ischemic DCM with marked variable expressivity. Coexisting BAG3 and FLNC variants should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than proof of dual-gene causality. The infection-associated acute decompensation, persistently normal cardiac injury biomarkers, non-ischemic LGE, and incomplete inflammatory CMR characterization favor cautious interpretation rather than a definitive diagnosis of myocarditis. Serial imaging, rhythm surveillance, individualized device-risk assessment, and follow-up of genotype-positive relatives are essential.

selected_papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. METHODS: A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. RESULTS: The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87-.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80-.87 and .80-.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1-6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. CONCLUSIONS: The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals. This low-cost tool could help reduce surveillance burden and facilitate earlier intervention.

selected_papers.abstract_full: Summary  Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is a severe heart condition often linked to arrhythmias, clots, and heart failure, for which treatments are not yet curative. Recently,  de novo mutations in genes encoding components of the Rag GTPase nutrient signaling pathway, particularly in  RRAGC , have been found in unrelated patients with a severe, early-onset DCM syndrome called Long-Olsen-Distelmaier. Cancer cell lines, hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and zebrafish have been used to study this  Ragopathy , but a mammalian model to investigate this syndrome has not been generated. Here, we show that mice engineered to endogenously express mutations in Serine 74 (orthologous to the Serine 75 mutated in patients), exhibit early-onset features of DCM with decreased heart size, fibrosis, diastolic dysfunction and aortic insufficiency, characteristics reminiscent of the human syndrome. Moreover,  Rragc -mutant hearts display decreased left ventricular mass and interventricular septum. Endogenous heterozygous expression of  Rragc mutant variants result in a milder, sublethal defective physiological cardiac growth with increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Mechanistically, active RagC does not cause abnormal increase in cardiomyocyte size, but leads to suppressed transcriptional activity of Tfeb and alterations in cardiomyocyte metabolism. Transcriptional profiling of neonatal mutant hearts reveals multiple signatures of impaired mitochondrial activity.  Ex vivo and  in vitro analyses of murine cardiomyocyte mitochondria from  Rragc -mutant mice show suppressed mitochondrial respiration, disturbed complex IV multimerization and super-complex organization. These data point to abnormal early postnatal heart metabolism by deregulated nutrient – Rag GTPase signaling with a potential molecular explanation to the early onset of DCM in patients with  de novo missense mutations in  RRAGC , and suggests the relevance of early metabolic interventions in conditions with altered nutrient signaling.
